fullText:
Flagstaff — A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced to two months in jail Wednesday for his role in a hazing that led to the death of a pledge.

Carter Eslick, 20, also received three years of supervised probation during a sentencing hearing in Coconino County Superior Court. Eslick had pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in the Jan. 31 death of Colin Daniel Martinez, 18, at an off-campus house.

An autopsy found Martinez died of alcohol poisoning with a blood-alcohol content of 0.425% — more than five times the state's legal limit for drivers 21 and over.

Martinez was among four Delta Tau Delta pledges who shared two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, according to court documents. Witnesses reported adjusting Martinez's sleeping position and checking his pulse and breathing to look for signs of alcohol poisoning throughout the night, the documents said.

Martinez's parents appeared remotely in court, still grieving their son, and said they want accountability and reform within Greek life, CBS Phoenix affiliate KPHO-TV reported.

Eslick was the fraternity's pledge master at the time and was responsible for welcoming new members.

The hearing began with testimony from five of Eslick's friends and family members who attested to his character while warning about the dangers of fraternity culture, KPHO noted.

"While trying to teach my children these things, I realized I failed to teach him or explain to them, and in those gaps, toxic influence and toxic communities have stepped in," said Cody Eslick, Carter's father.

Carter Eslick apologized to Martinez's family, KPHO said.

"I am so incredibly deeply sorry for the events that happened on Jan. 31, and I take full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual," Eslick said. "And if I had known that one day somebody's life could be in my hands, there is no way in hell I would have ever looked that way."

Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said no sentence can undo the harm to the Martinez family.

"My hope is that this case helps people understand the serious dangers of hazing and encourages them to speak up and intervene before another family experiences this kind of loss," Barker said in a statement.

Judge Stacy Krueger said Eslick knew what he did was dangerous and was troubled that no one spoke out against it.

Eslick could face additional jail time if he doesn't meet the conditions of probation, which include creating and delivering 305 anti-hazing presentations and keeping the court updated on his progress. He also can't use alcohol or drugs unless prescribed.

The university suspended the fraternity after Martinez's death, and the national organization later closed the NAU chapter.

title: Judge permanently dismisses Reflecting Pool vandalism case against ex-Olympian
description:
— A judge in the nation's capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn's case with "prejudice," which would block U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A judge in the nation's capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.

D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn's case with "prejudice," which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office from refiling the felony charge against him. The judge ruled nearly a month after hearing attorneys' arguments.

Hearn's lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro's decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro "choked" and "folded like an umbrella."

Edelman said the case presents "exceptional circumstances" that warrant dismissing the case permanently. He agreed with defense attorneys that the government "shot first and asked questions later" by charging Hearn in a "a lightning-fast indictment process."

"While the government wishes to hold open the possibility of the development of evidence that would support a future prosecution, its own representations make plain that such a possibility is theoretical at best, and more likely, is simply fanciful," the judge wrote.

Permanently dismissing the case protects Hearn from prosecutors electing to revive the case under political pressure from Trump, the judge said.

"Although the prosecutors assigned to this case have deemed it meritless, the President of the United States has repeatedly disparaged them and pressured them to change course," Edelman wrote.

In a court filing in July, Pirro said new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed Hearn wasn't responsible for damage to the pool's lining. Pirro's office attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer's America 250 celebration in Washington.

Pirro's admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump's claims that vandals damaged the pool.

Hearn has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool's newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker's command to let go of it.

Hearn was charged with one count of property destruction, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.

Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.

Trump, a Republican, appointed Pirro, a former Fox News host, to serve as the top federal prosecutor for the District of Columbia. Edelman was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama.

Hearn's attorneys said the ruling is "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice" and allows Hearn to "move forward with his life as he deserves."

"This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted," the lawyers said in a statement.

fullText:
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.

The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.

Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.

In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.

"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.

Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.

He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".

But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.

Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".

Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.

Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.

Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents.

Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself.

"If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said.

"There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them."

Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI.

"There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said.

So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon.

"At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

fullText:
Trump defended such a move, saying Biden "gave pardons to everyone."

President Donald Trump said in an interview out Thursday that he would be open to pardoning members of his administration, pointing to former President Joe Biden’s blanket pardon to relatives and members of the administration out of concern they would be politically targeted after he left office.

"Yeah, sure, I'd do that," the president answered when asked by TIME magazine earlier this week if he was "considering pardoning members of your administration prior to the end of your term?"

The president further said that Biden "gave pardons to everyone."

Biden issued preemptive pardons to several close family members in the final minutes of his presidency in 2025, saying that his family "has been subjected to unrelenting attacks and threats, motivated solely by a desire to hurt me" and that he had "no reason to believe these attacks will end" after he left office.

Those pardons included James Biden, Joe's younger brother; Sara Jones Biden, James' wife; Valerie Biden Owens, Joe's younger sister; John T. Owens', Valerie's husband; and Francis W. Biden, Joe's younger brother.

In 2024, Biden pardoned his son, Hunter Biden, who was convicted on tax evasion and federal gun charges.

Trump's pardon comments mark the first time he has publicly said he would consider pardoning members of his administration.

Last year, he issued pardons to some to his political and financial supporters as well as several high-profile individuals allegedly involved in his attempt to overturn the election. In his first term, he pardoned several advisers, members of his campaign and one former member of his administration, former National Security Advisor Michael Flynn.

In the interview, Trump expressed his belief that if the Democrats emerge victorious in the midterm elections, “they'll probably go after" him, but he said he will also target them back.

Trump still expressed confidence that Republicans will "do okay" in November, as long as he is on the campaign trail.

"No, I think we'll do okay if I campaign, and I intend to," he said, when asked if he believes that Democrats will take control of Congress.

He then went on to tout some of his endorsement victories including for Republicans Darline Graham and Ed Gallerin -- who defeated Rep. Thomas Massie in the primary for Kentucky’s 4th Congressional District.

Asked about his record low poll numbers, Trump called them "fake" and insisted that he could easily beat anybody who ran against him.

"They're fake numbers. I would beat anybody running today by 20 points," Trump said. "Your numbers that you have are fake."

Trump's cover of TIME magazine will mark his 56th such appearance, according to the outlet. That's more than any other figure in history, surpassing former President Richard Nixon's record.

Trump's interview will be the cover story for TIME's Oct. 26 issue.

   "Yeah.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Oct 1 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said he regretted nominating three Supreme Court justices — Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett and ‌Brett Kavanaugh — who have opposed him in recent rulings, according ‌to a Time Magazine interview.

The Republican president was asked about his recent comments regarding the ​three conservative justices in the interview, which was conducted on Monday.

"Do you regret nominating them?" the interviewer asked, referring to Trump's comments in a recent Truth Social post.

"Yeah. Yeah," Trump responded, according to a transcript of the ‌interview.

"What can I do? ⁠I put them in. They voted against me too often. I was very — I gave them the position of ⁠a lifetime, and they vote against me often."

Trump appointed Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett during his first term as president, building a 6-3 conservative majority and allowing the court ​to steer ​a dramatic rightward course since 2020.

"I ​do like loyalty, yeah," Trump ‌told the interviewer, who then asked whether that was what he wanted from the justices.

"No, I don't want loyalty. I want good decisions," Trump said.

After the top US judicial body declined to allow a Postal Service rule restricting the use of mail-in ballots in the November midterm elections, ‌Trump said his appointees were behaving differently ​than they had during interviews.

"These are not ​the people I interviewed to ​serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are ‌merely a shell of their original ​selves," he wrote on ​Truth Social.

After the court in February struck down his sweeping global tariffs that it found he had imposed illegally using a ​law meant for national ‌emergencies, Trump reserved special ire for Gorsuch and Barrett, who were in ​the majority in that 6-3 ruling.

title: Pentagon used emergency measure to change voter forms for Americans abroad
description:
Democrats filed a lawsuit Thursday over the Trump administration’s recent use of an emergency measure to make changes to the federal voter-registration form used by U.S. service members abroad and citizens residing outside the country, arguing that it’s an attempt to disenfranchise eligible American voters.
The lawsuit follows concerns by advocates for American citizens overseas, who said the changes will spark confusion among eligible voters abroad and officials within U.S.
fullText:
Democrats filed a lawsuit Thursday over the Trump administration's recent use of an emergency measure to make changes to the federal voter-registration form used by U.S. service members abroad and citizens residing outside the country, arguing that it's an attempt to disenfranchise eligible American voters.

The lawsuit follows concerns by advocates for American citizens overseas, who said the changes will spark confusion among eligible voters abroad and officials within U.S. election offices. The Pentagon has saidthe changes are meant to align the form with federal law. More than 2 million Americans living abroad are eligible to cast their ballots in U.S. elections.

The new version of the form changes ID requirements and eliminates a checkbox that allows a voter to declare, "I am a US citizen living outside the country, I have never lived in the United States." That category, sometimes referred to as "never resideds," encompasses the adult children of U.S. citizens who have long lived abroad.

The Democratic National Committee's lawsuit against the Pentagon and the Office of Management and Budget argues that the federal government manufactured an emergency to justify infringing on the voting rights of "never resideds." The DNC is asking the court to declare that the agencies acted unlawfully, stop the federal government from distributing the recently altered version of the form and direct the Pentagon to reissue a previous version of the form.

Doris Speer, president of the Association of Americans Resident Overseas, said she believes the changes to the form, known as the Federal Post Card Application, are "an effort to deter the overseas vote, not to legally stop people from voting but to make the process so difficult that you really have to want to vote to get through it. The result will be confusion, chaos and fewer overseas votes."

The changes to the form follow the Trump administration's unsuccessful efforts to restrict voting by mail and pass sweeping voter ID legislation. That proposed legislation, the Save America Act, would require Americans to prove their citizenship when registering to vote and show photo ID to vote, and permit the Department of Homeland Security to obtain access to voter rolls.

The political stakes of the upcoming midterm election are high for the GOP. Republicans are in danger of losing their majority in the House of Representatives, and Democrats have vowed to step up their investigations into President Donald Trump if they are in the majority.

In August, the Pentagon sought emergency approval to make several changes to the FPCA, used by U.S. voters abroad to register to vote and request an absentee ballot. The Pentagon did not solicit public feedback on the change, as normally would be a part of the process for a document change of this nature.

The Pentagon told The Washington Post in a statement that recent updates were made "to streamline voter identification instructions and ensure alignment with Federal law" but did not detail which federal law. The Pentagon also did not explain what emergency allowed the government to expedite the form changes.

In an Aug. 13 letter to OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs seeking emergency processing to alter the form, Deputy Undersecretary of War for Personnel and Readiness Sean O'Keefe wrote that the changes were necessary because the previous version of the document may have confused "voters about the information they are required to provide under Federal law and their eligibility to use these forms to register and vote."

In justifying the emergency, O'Keefe wrote that "the next Federal election is fewer than 90 days away, so there is insufficient time to modify" the forms via the standard process, adding that "public harm is reasonably likely to result if normal clearance procedures and time periods are followed."

Elections are typically scheduled years in advance. Tammy Patrick, a longtime elections administrator who serves as the chief program officer at the National Association of Election Officials, and other advocates for U.S. voters overseas say they still don't understand what constituted an emergency in this case.

"I don't think there is an actual emergency," Patrick said. "I have not heard from any election officials about anything related to our infrastructure, neither at the state level … nor at any local level, causing any major concern within our hundreds and hundreds of members."

A 1986 law established federal protections for military and overseas voters. But states determine voter eligibility rules and residence requirements. Currently, "never resideds" are eligible to vote in 37 states based on their parents' previous residence.

Along with changes to the form itself, the General Services Administration's website for the newly altered form also states that it "is for absent Uniform Service members, their families, and citizens residing outside the U.S. intending on returning only." Previously, the federal government made no distinction on who was eligible to use the form based on whether an American citizen intended to return to the United States.

Susan Dzieduszycka-Suinat, president and CEO of the nonprofit U.S. Vote Foundation, said that changing the form "without an effective public comment process sends a terrible message to the people who have always been part of it: election officials, usability experts, and organizations like ours. That process used to give us a form that supported voter participation and made life easier for election administrators."

Speer, with the Association of Americans Resident Overseas, said she wasn't interested in mounting a legal fight ahead of the midterm election, arguing that any effort to stop the federal government from using the new form could create even more confusion for voters. But Dzieduszycka-Suinat said U.S. Vote Foundation is "investigating this issue and the emergency process that was used with legal counsel." She said the organization is prepared to fight in court.

Eligible "never resided" voters must now seek their ballots through states, rather than through the federal government.

California, for example, is one of 37 states that allow a U.S. citizen who never has lived in the United States to vote if their parent or legal guardian was previously registered to vote as a resident of the state. The California secretary of state's office told The Post that the state's online voter-registration application continues to include a category for U.S. citizens who "have never resided in the U.S."

title: Layoffs are down, but employers aren't rushing to hire for the holidays
description:
New applications for US unemployment benefits drifted close to 57-year lows last week and layoffs decreased in September, suggesting labor market stability persisted even as employers remained cautious about boosting hiring. 
   The report from the Labor Department on Thursday joined a raft of other data, including robust consumer spending in August, in painting a rosy picture of the economy despite ‌rising headwinds from the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has driven diesel prices to record highs. Economists said robust corporate profits growth and resilient domestic demand were shielding workers from layoffs, for now. 
   "At some point, ‌elevated energy costs and material prices will force firms to lay off marginal workers to protect profit margins, but there is no sign of that here," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics. 
   Initial claims for state unemployment benefits slipped 1,000 to a seasonally adjusted 197,000 for ​the week ended September 26, the Labor Department said on Thursday.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Oct 1 (Reuters) - New applications for US unemployment benefits drifted close to 57-year lows last week and layoffs decreased in September, suggesting labor market stability persisted even as employers remained cautious about boosting hiring.

The report from the Labor Department on Thursday joined a raft of other data, including robust consumer spending in August, in painting a rosy picture of the economy despite ‌rising headwinds from the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has driven diesel prices to record highs. Economists said robust corporate profits growth and resilient domestic demand were shielding workers from layoffs, for now.

"At some point, ‌elevated energy costs and material prices will force firms to lay off marginal workers to protect profit margins, but there is no sign of that here," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits slipped 1,000 to a seasonally adjusted 197,000 for ​the week ended September 26, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 200,000 claims for the latest week.

Claims have held below the 200,000 level for three straight weeks and are near levels last seen in 1969. Some economists said historically low layoffs, if sustained, could raise questions about the labor market overheating, with monetary policy implications.

"We do not appear to be close to that result yet, but this is a new risk that the FOMC appears to be watching," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets, referring to the Fed's policy-setting committee.

A separate report from global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas showed layoffs announced by US-based employers dropped 18% to 43,281 in September. They were down 20% ‌from a year ago and fell 43% in the third quarter. Employers are, however, ⁠in no rush to increase headcount.

Hiring plans increased by 90,787 last month. While that was sharply up from 12,325 in August, hiring intentions were down 23% from a year ago, and the tally was the lowest for any September since 2011. Challenger, Gray & Christmas said a surge in seasonal hiring typically seen starting in September was absent, adding that "companies are in ⁠a wait-and-see period."

The Federal Reserve last month raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, the first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. The odds of another rate hike this month were diminished by cooler-than-expected inflation readings in August and July.

title: Judge denies Lindsay Clancy's bid to dismiss murder case, clearing path for retrial
description:
A Massachusetts judge has denied Lindsay Clancy’s attempt to have the murder charges against her thrown out, clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue a retrial in the high-profile case involving the deaths of her three children.
In a ruling issued Thursday, Plymouth Superior Court Judge William F. Sullivan rejected the defense’s Rule 25 motion for a required finding of not guilty following September’s mistrial. Under Massachusetts law, a Rule 25 motion asks a judge to determine whether prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to convict. 
Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued the Commonwealth failed to prove two key elements of its case: that Clancy killed her three children and that she was criminally responsible for her actions at the time.
fullText:
A Massachusetts judge has denied Lindsay Clancy's attempt to have the murder charges against her thrown out, clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue a retrial in the high-profile case involving the deaths of her three children.

In a ruling issued Thursday, Plymouth Superior Court Judge William F. Sullivan rejected the defense's Rule 25 motion for a required finding of not guilty following September's mistrial. Under Massachusetts law, a Rule 25 motion asks a judge to determine whether prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to convict.

Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued the Commonwealth failed to prove two key elements of its case: that Clancy killed her three children and that she was criminally responsible for her actions at the time.

Sullivan disagreed, finding that prosecutors presented enough evidence for a reasonable jury to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy committed the killings and could be held criminally responsible.

“There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder," Sullivan wrote.

The decision does not determine guilt or innocence. Rather, it means the judge found the evidence presented during the first trial was legally sufficient for the case to proceed to a new jury.

The ruling represents a victory for prosecutors, who have maintained that Clancy carefully planned the killings of her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, on January 24, 2023, then tried to kill herself, while her husband was briefly out of the family's Duxbury home.

Newsweek has contacted Reddington by email and left a message with Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy J. Cruz's office seeking comment.

According to the decision, prosecutors introduced both physical and circumstantial evidence showing that Clancy was alone with the children during the relevant time period. Her husband, Patrick Clancy, testified that he left the house to pick up takeout food and medication and later returned to find evidence of violence inside the home before discovering his children in the basement.

Medical examiners testified that the children died from asphyxia or complications resulting from mechanical asphyxia. Prosecutors alleged the children were strangled with exercise bands.

The judge also rejected the defense's challenge to the state's evidence regarding criminal responsibility. During the trial, both sides agreed that Clancy suffered from a serious mental illness at the time. The central dispute was whether that illness rendered her legally incapable of appreciating the wrongfulness of her conduct or conforming her behavior to the law.

Sullivan noted that three prosecution experts testified that Clancy retained those capacities, even if defense experts reached different conclusions. Resolving those competing opinions, he wrote, is a matter for a jury rather than a judge.

Thursday's decision marks the second time Sullivan has rejected the defense's bid to dismiss the case, finding on both occasions that prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a jury to consider the charges.

“For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this,” Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told the judge during Tuesday's hearing. “I’d suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this.”

A hearing is scheduled for November 2, when the parties are expected to address several unresolved issues, including Clancy's motion to block a retrial on double jeopardy grounds and the defense's request for a court inquiry into Michael Desronvil, the

Defense attorneys have sought scrutiny of Desronvil's phone records as part of their effort to investigate the circumstances surrounding the mistrial and the conduct of the jury's deliberations.

Paul Mauro, an attorney and Fox News contributor, wrote on X after Sullivan's ruling, "Unsurprising. He should similarly swat down the double jeopardy motion and the request to review the holdout juror's phone."

Prosecutors have not yet said whether they intend to retry Clancy. Their options include pursuing another first-degree murder case, seeking lesser charges such as second-degree murder or manslaughter, or declining to move forward altogether.

If a retrial is ordered, a new jury would once again be asked to decide whether Clancy is guilty of murdering her three children or whether her mental state at the time rendered her not criminally responsible.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.

title: Early voting data shows emerging signs of a Democratic advantage in the midterms
description:
"I Voted" stickers sit on a table at Naperville Municipal Center in Naperville, Illinois, on September 24, 2026, on the first day of early voting ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. - Kamil Krzaczyski/AFP/Getty Images
Election Day is still a month away, but more than 700,000 Americans have already voted across at least 30 states. There are signs emerging of the advantage Democrats have in motivating their voters – a trend that’s played out in polling all summer long.
In several states with key Senate or governor races this fall, Democrats make up a larger share of voters requesting ballots so far than they did at this point in 2024.
In Iowa, Democrats have made 67% of ballot requests, up from 54% at this point in 2024.
fullText:
Election Day is still a month away, but more than 700,000 Americans have already voted across at least 30 states. There are signs emerging of the advantage Democrats have in motivating their voters – a trend that’s played out in polling all summer long.

In several states with key Senate or governor races this fall, Democrats make up a larger share of voters requesting ballots so far than they did at this point in 2024.

In Iowa, Democrats have made 67% of ballot requests, up from 54% at this point in 2024. In Pennsylvania, it’s 66%, up from 62%, and in Maine it’s 57%, up from 53%. And according to data from the North Carolina State Board of Elections, 42% of ballot requests are from Democrats, up from 36% at this point two years ago.

It’s worth noting that in all of those states except for Iowa, ballot requests at this point in 2022 were more Democratic than they are now.

The uptick in the share of requests from Democrats would be in line with polling, special election results and primary turnout, all of which have indicated Democrats may be more motivated to vote this November.

On the other hand, it could just be further evidence of Republicans continuing to shift to preferring other forms of voting.

An important caveat: While the fact that a person has voted is generally public information, your ballot itself is secret, so this data can’t tell us how many votes a party or candidate has won. That won’t be known until states start reporting results after the polls close on November 3.

Early voting data also only shows one slice of voters: a slice that is typically older and less Republican than the electorate as a whole.

As mail voting has fallen from its 2020 highs, voters 65 and older have made up a larger share of people choosing to vote that way, going from 27% of mail voters in 2020 to 31% in 2022 and 37% in 2024, according to CNN Exit Poll data.

That’s not unexpected. Mail voting can be a convenient option for older people who might have trouble getting to the polls. In many states where voters need an excuse to vote by mail, age itself can qualify as a reason to receive a mail-in ballot.

There are early signs that that trend is continuing this year.

In nearly every state for which there is comparable data, voters 65 and older make up a larger share of ballot requests this year than they did at this point in either 2022 or 2024.

Perhaps the most positive signs for Democrats so far come from Virginia, which has reported both by far the most total votes of any state in CNN’s count and is the only state which has reported substantial numbers of both early in-person and mail votes.

While Virginia voters don’t register by party, there’s a clear relationship between how a locality voted in 2024 and its relative pace of early voting.

Cities and counties that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris by more than 20 percentage points are at 78% of their turnout from this time in 2024, while those that voted for President Donald Trump by 20 points are at just 61%.

Partisan turnout, as measured by the share of voters who have only participated in one party’s primaries since 2022, also points to a considerable Democratic advantage in the early voting period relative to the same point in 2024.

While the turnout so far shows a clear advantage in Democratic motivation, Republican voters could close the gap as Election Day nears. It’s still early in the voting period – Virginians cast over 4.5 million votes in 2024 and over 3.4 million votes in 2025. The Senate race in Virginia is not expected to be competitive this year, and Republican voters may be more motivated in more highly contested races.

Still, two competitive House races in the state also suggest a move towards Democrats in terms of enthusiasm.

Democratic primary participants outnumber Republican primary participants by 15 points among votes cast so far in the 1st District and 18 points in the 2nd District. Both districts are battlegrounds currently represented by Republicans facing tough challengers: Rep. Rob Wittman in the 1st and Rep. Jen Kiggans in the 2nd.

At the same point in 2024, the partisan composition was relatively split in both districts, with Republican primary voters leading by about 3 points in the 1st District and Democratic primary voters leading by 2 points in the 2nd District.

Statewide, Democratic primary participants outpace Republicans by about 18 points, up from 8 points at the same point in 2024.

Data on pre-election voting is valuable but it does have limits.

Early vote data is compiled by CNN, the Associated Press, and the data firm Catalist, a company that provides data, analytics and other services to Democrats, academics and nonprofit advocacy groups, including insights into who is voting before November.

The number of votes cast so far is a tiny fraction of the roughly 57 million pre-election votes cast in 2022 and an even smaller share of the roughly 112 million votes cast overall in that election but is expected to grow substantially over the next few weeks.

The data so far is also largely limited to mail ballots, as very few states have started significant early in-person voting. In recent years mail voters have been much more Democratic, while early in-person voters have been more evenly split or Republican leaning.

This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring
description:
Xbox, PC (version tested); The Coalition/Xbox Game Studios
E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Every Gears of War game released in the last 20 years has made reverent reference to Emergence Day, when alien creatures emerged from the earth, single-minded in their savagery. In E-Day, you’re there to witness it: the police lights, flipped cars, ground tremors, civilians running, aliens pouring out of fissures in the earth and ripping faces off. You’re at ground zero in a squad of four soldiers called Gears – Marcus Fenix, the leader; Dom, who wants to retire; Lucas, a green cadet with a buzzcut; and the dishonourably discharged Mags. Only this dysfunctional quartet can turn the tide. With guns.
fullText:
Xbox, PC (version tested); The Coalition/Xbox Game Studios
E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing

Every Gears of War game released in the last 20 years has made reverent reference to Emergence Day, when alien creatures emerged from the earth, single-minded in their savagery. In E-Day, you’re there to witness it: the police lights, flipped cars, ground tremors, civilians running, aliens pouring out of fissures in the earth and ripping faces off. You’re at ground zero in a squad of four soldiers called Gears – Marcus Fenix, the leader; Dom, who wants to retire; Lucas, a green cadet with a buzzcut; and the dishonourably discharged Mags. Only this dysfunctional quartet can turn the tide. With guns. Lots of ’em.

Instead of answering questions raised by the ending of 2019’s Gears 5, we’re back to the start to find out why Marcus has a scar on his lip and why these soldiers started strapping chainsaws on to their assault rifles. Anything that was left to the imagination is here, for you to point at and say: “I understood that reference. This is a thing that I have seen.”

This series has lost its way a bit over the years, but the opening hours of E-Day will have you believing that big shoulder pads and ripping into gollum-esque freaks with motor-powered blades are en vogue once again. There are flashes of the horror and grimness of the first couple of Gears games as you’re funnelled between urban fighting arenas, with bountiful flanking routes and chunks of fallen buildings to take cover behind. But then it keeps going. And going. Long after you realise it’s all out of ideas, it’s still going.

Because it’s set during and immediately after E-Day, the squad is stuck. You spend most of your time running back and forth across the city in various states of destruction. You cross the same section of bridge three times before the credits roll. Levels are flipped, daytime turns to night and you run through them again. E-Day’s two attempts at switching things up involve putting you on the gunner seat of a helicopter or making you walk slowly while people talk to you. The setting is a ball and chain that the developers are tethered to.

E-Day is at its best when it turns off the lights, cranks up the horror, and forces you into enclosed spaces, but these moments make up a tiny portion of the game. The bulk of it is spent in large, open areas stuffed to the gills with collectibles. There are hundreds of them and you get a little audio chime whenever one is close. At one point, there was a particularly poignant cutscene where one of the emotionally stunted characters finally lets it all out and, just as the game transitioned from this emotional beat back to gameplay, the chime drowned out the character’s trauma to tell me there was something to pick up nearby.

These open levels are big enough to require a map to navigate and they’re even peppered with side objectives (usually mini horde missions where you hold off waves of enemies after setting up defences). In Gears 5, you at least had a vehicle to zip between points of interest. Here you’re just hoofing it on foot, trying to cover as much of the map as possible without triggering the next cutscene. If you do happen to stray into the main objective by accident and try to backtrack, you’re hit with a big “mission failed” message for stepping out of bounds. You basically die. For exploring. In a game that constantly tells you to explore.

It’s a shame because if you rip a chainsaw through all the fat and wipe the blood spray from your eyes, there’s good meat on the bones here. Combat-wise, this is the best the series has ever felt. Characters move much less clunkily, heaving into cover, sliding under chunks of rubble, even leaping around with grace that the older Marcus Fenix and his creaky knees could only dream of.

Environments crack and splinter as you fight, with glass smashing into shards that litter on the ground. Cars wobble as they take a hit, petrol stations explode and pillars crumble like the Matrix corridor scene. Blood and entrails cover everything when the dust settles after a firefight.

Cover feels more naturalistic and combat arenas blend nicely into the open sections, blurring the lines between exploration and fighting elegantly. Guns feel hefty and dangerous – especially the shotgun that spits acid. Active reloading, which asks you to time a button press for faster weapon reloads and more powerful bullets, remains a smart bit of game design that keeps you locked in as you fight.

There’s a reason Gears of War has survived as a series long enough to earn a prequel. Its specific flavour of bloody, tactical, cover-based combat isn’t done better anywhere else. Unfortunately, E-Day is let down by everything around that fighting, resulting in a safe and repetitive experience that shows you all its ideas in the opening hours and never dares to build on them in any meaningful way.

title: Anthropic pushes for opt-out model for Australian content as ABC warns of ‘cannibalisation’ of news
description: Maker of Claude claims AI could transform economy but ABC and SBS say the technology should be subject to media...
fullText:
Maker of Claude claims AI could transform economy but ABC and SBS say the technology should be subject to media regulations

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The AI giant Anthropic has urged the Albanese government to consider giving “conditional approval” for big tech to train its models on Australian copyrighted works under an opt-out model, after conceding it won’t secure a blanket copyright exemption.

But Australia’s public broadcasters, the ABC and SBS, have strongly criticised AI firms, calling on the government to enact strict new rules to compensate media organisations and protect public interest journalism.

In submissions to a federal parliamentary inquiry, the ABC demanded AI companies be subject to the same copyright, defamation and privacy rules as media outlets, warning of a “cannibalisation” of mainstream news.

The ABC and SBS also suggested the government include AI companies in the news bargaining incentive, which would require them to make commercial deals with large media outlets to support journalism.

“As publishers, AI-based services are currently unregulated and receive more favourable treatment than established Australian media. This unequal treatment will accelerate the cannibalisation of the Australian news industry,” the ABC said in its submission.

SBS said AI-powered large language models – such as ChatGPT or Claude – were “challenges to the sustainability of the Australian news industry and the erosion of information integrity and public trust through their use of news content without permission, attribution or compensation”.

The joint select committee on AI will hold a series of hearings in Sydney next week, with executives from Anthropic to attend along with those from OpenAI, after it admitted one of its AI agents had accessed Services Australia data in June.

In a newly published submission, Anthropic said there was “light and shade” to be considered around the development of AI. It claimed the technology could “transform the Australian economy, drive a new wave of productivity” and “solve some of the nation’s biggest challenges”, but also warned of “serious implications for Australia’s national security, the resilience of its critical infrastructure and the safety of its people”.

The company talked up its plans for investing billions in Australia, including large new datacentres, and urged the government to support “frontier model training”. But one sticking point raised by AI companies has been access to Australian copyrighted works – such as news, books, music and other written material – to help train AI models.

The Labor government has ruled out a so-called text and data mining exemption, with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, promising “the strongest possible protection” for Australian creatives. But questions have lingered about other possible copyright changes and the suggestion of an opt-out measure, allowing copyright holders to choose whether their content can be accessed by AI companies.

Anthropic’s submission called on Australia to “provide legal certainty under copyright that brings AI developers to the table while advancing its national cultural interests”.

“Anthropic accepts that broad exceptions from copyright, such as a text and data mining exception, have not received widespread support and have been ruled out by the Government. As an alternative, we believe that the Government could permit AI model training through a narrow form of conditional approval,” the company submitted.

It suggested the implementation of “do not crawl” signals through robots.txt files – which tell bots what they may and may not access – and said the company was “open” to supporting Australian creators.

However SBS said that such an opt-out measure may not work.

“Robots.txt mechanisms are routinely ignored or bypassed, and the blocking of ever-evolving training bots increases the burden on rightsholders to monitor and update protections, when the onus should be on AI companies to avoid wrongdoing,” the broadcaster said in its submission.

The ABC complained that AI companies did not abide by the same rules as media outlets, calling the current system “anti-competitive”.

Both broadcasters called for AI to be included in the news bargaining incentive – with which big tech platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Google, TikTok and Snapchat have been forced to comply.

title: California issues investigative subpoena to OpenAI over rogue agents’ hacking
description:
State attorney general issues subpoena to OpenAI as ​part of broader inquiry into potential security vulnerabilities
California’s attorney general has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI, starting an investigation into the startup ⁠as ​part of a broader inquiry into potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents related ⁠to its AI models, his office said on Thursday.
Last month, Rob Bonta announced that ⁠the Department of Justice was conducting a formal ​investigation into the “Hugging ‌Face incident”, amid increasing ‌scrutiny of the AI industry. AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked Hugging Face in July, gaining access to parts of the open-source platform’s infrastructure.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
State attorney general issues subpoena to OpenAI as ​part of broader inquiry into potential security vulnerabilities

California’s attorney general has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI, starting an investigation into the startup ⁠as ​part of a broader inquiry into potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents related ⁠to its AI models, his office said on Thursday.

Last month, Rob Bonta announced that ⁠the Department of Justice was conducting a formal ​investigation into the “Hugging ‌Face incident”, amid increasing ‌scrutiny of the AI industry. AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked Hugging Face in July, gaining access to parts of the open-source platform’s infrastructure.

“My office is ​asking ​OpenAI additional questions ​regarding cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the ​company and ‌its AI models,” ​Bonta said ​in a statement.

OpenAI did not ‌immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Federal Trade Commission is ‌conducting an industry-wide investigation into Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI labs to uncover ​the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers. The investigation is the first official US enforcement action ⁠that delves into rogue AI agents.

Bonta warned that developers failing to uphold this responsibility could face legal accountability.

title: Google rolls out new Gemini AI model but restricts access over safety concerns
description: Tech company releases Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by...
fullText:
Tech company releases Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers

Google on Wednesday said it would withhold its most powerful artificial intelligence model from the public for now, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers.

“Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach,” wrote Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google’s chief AI architect, in a blogpost announcing the model.

Google said it was voluntarily giving the US government early access to the model and would gather feedback from testers before making it widely available.

The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rival Anthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a small number of trusted organizations.

Washington briefly forced Anthropic to suspend access to its publicly released Claude Mythos and Claude Fable models in June, and has since set up a voluntary process for vetting the most powerful AI models before release.

The announcement came a day after Donald Trump hosted top tech executives, including the Google chief, Sundar Pichai, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, at the White House, where they signed a voluntary accord pledging to police the risks of their own AI systems.

Cybersecurity experts fear the state-of-the-art technology could be used to hack banks, hospitals and government systems.

Google said Argon excelled at complex tasks in software engineering, legal and financial work and cyber-defense, with a leading ability to find and fix critical software flaws.

Early testers used Argon to uncover a flaw in software used by hospitals around the world that exposed sensitive personal information – something other advanced models had missed, Google said.

Google said Argon was designed to refuse requests that could help carry out cyber-attacks or develop chemical, biological or nuclear weapons.

Anthropic and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI have built similar safeguards into their most advanced models.

Google said it was monitoring the model’s reasoning to stop it from straying beyond what users intended, a risk researchers call misalignment.

The issue has taken on new urgency since OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models, including one not yet released, broke out of a sealed test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked into the servers of the AI company Hugging Face.

You Could Lose Your Access to 'Old Reddit' Forever, but There's a Workaround
description: The company is putting extreme limits on Old Reddit.
fullText:
"Old Reddit" is the only way I use Reddit. That's not the case for most of the tech in my life. I don't make a point of only using an iPhone from a decade ago, or avoid playing video games with more than 64 bits. But, in my view, Old Reddit is the only proper way to use the website. While "new" Reddit has more "features," it's bloated and slow. Old Reddit might be extremely basic, and looks about the same as it did when I first started "redditing," but it works. Unfortunately, most of us likely won't be able to experience Old Reddit for much longer.

On Wednesday, Reddit announced a series of infrastructure changes on its r/modnews subreddit. Normally, these updates wouldn't make tech headlines—I can't say Reddit "mod news" often finds its way into my feeds. But as part of these changes, Reddit confirmed a rather massive deprecation: Users will lose access to Old Reddit unless they've used the platform sometime in the last six months. It's not enough to use Reddit itself, mind you: Unless you use Old Reddit at least once in a six-month period, you'll lose access for good.

This builds on a previous Old Reddit change the company rolled out over the summer, which requires users to be logged in in order to access this version of Reddit. While we don't have a true deadline for when these new changes take effect, the new announcement makes it clear that, "in the next few months, we’ll further limit access for logged-in users to only those who have used Old Reddit in the last six months (which covers the vast majority of all Old Reddit users).” The only exception is for moderators.

According to Reddit, these changes are designed to prevent abuse on its platform. By forcing users to log in to use Old Reddit, the company says it prevents unauthenticated access, its "largest source of abusive scraping and automated traffic." By blocking accounts that haven't accessed Old Reddit in the past six months, Reddit says it's solving another problem: Now, bad actors won't be able to make Reddit accounts for the sole purpose of accessing (and scraping) Old Reddit and its content.

In Reddit's view, these changes don't affect Old Reddit users. If you rely on Old Reddit, the company thinks you'll be using it frequently enough to bypass these new rules. As such, Reddit believes the vast majority of affected users will only be those trying to abuse Old Reddit, not those who actively use it.

The problem is, not everyone who uses Old Reddit is so steadfast. These new rules mean you can no longer take an extended break from Old Reddit and expect to return in the future. Sure, Reddit will always be there, but you'll lose access to the "best" version of the platform, as so many believe it to be. As this is the second change to Old Reddit in a short period of time, it begs the question: Is Reddit trying to shut down Old Reddit? That's what Ars Technica asked the company, and received the following in response:

"As [Reddit CEO Steve Huffman previously] confirmed, Reddit is continuing to work on the future of Old Reddit. This change is about limiting unauthenticated access and reducing automated abuse—not removing Old Reddit for people and moderators who rely on it. We want to preserve Old Reddit for the real people that use it, not let it be a vector for automated abuse."

Per the rules, the easiest way to continue using Old Reddit is to simply keep using it. If you've never done so before, you can head to old.reddit.com and sign into your account when prompted. As long as you access this version of the site at least once every six months, you'll maintain your access—assuming Reddit doesn't change the rules again.

But if you want a more permanent fix without having to worry about visiting Old Reddit twice a year, become a mod. Moderators don't have the same requirements; simply being a mod gives them perpetual access to the site. The easiest way to become a mod is to simply start your own subreddit. If you have access to Old Reddit, you'll see this on the front page as "Create your own subreddit." If you're on new Reddit, you'll see this as "Start a community" under the three-lined menu. Reddit will walk you through the rest, asking you to answer questions or fill out responses about your new community. Assuming the subreddit isn't already taken, you'll be able to create it at the end, at which point you will automatically become a mod of your new subreddit.

Why You Shouldn't Expect a Tiny Kindle Any Time Soon
description: Never say never, but right now, smaller e-readers don't fit with Amazon's brand.
fullText:
Earlier this week, I commented that the recent boom in tiny e-readers—I'm talking about those credit card-sized, Chinese-made e-ink devices that have become all the rage on BookTok and Reddit—was the most interesting thing to happen to e-readers in years. From the Xteink X4 Pro to the forthcoming Boox Picco, these wee little guys, which are small enough to slip into any pocket, have gathered a cult following of readers who prize ultra-portability above all else.

Today's announcement of a redesigned line of Kindles didn't do anything to change that opinion. Setting aside the additional reveal of long-requested accessories like a Bluetooth page-turn remote and a charging dock, these new Kindles mostly deliver the same familiar Amazon e-reader experience in a slightly more refined package. And if you were hoping Amazon might hop on the bandwagon with a tiny e-reader of its own—or even a phone-shaped e-reader like the Boox Palma— well, I wouldn't hold your breath.

Yesterday, Amazon invited other journalists and me to the company's New York City headquarters to check out the new Kindles, and during our talk with Kevin Keith, vice president of the Kindle team, we asked him if the company has been monitoring the pocket e-reader trend, and if it would ever make a Kindle with a screen smaller than the standard six inches. His response didn't surprise me at all.

"Our answer to that is, I think [the basic Kindle]—when you're at 140 grams, and you're this lightweight, you can carry it almost anywhere. I carry these in my pocket. In your bag, you're not even going to know it's there," Keith said. "I think that's first and foremost what I'd say." That is, Amazon already thinks the six-inch device is plenty small enough for most readers, and as a company, Amazon is generally targeting most readers. The tiny e-reader audience is "a very vocal group of people," he added, "but I don't know how big that group of people is."

While it's monitoring the chatter around devices like the Palma or even smaller options like the X4 Pro, for Amazon, the existing entry-level Kindle is "a really good format," Keith said. "Getting to four or five inches, I think there's just a lot of compromises there that you have to make. The core answer is just making a better entry device."

Chris Green, Kindle's vice president of design, a veteran who has worked on every Kindle device save the first-generation model (which was released just as he joined the company), agreed, while leaving the door open just a crack wider: "I think they're fascinating," Green said of smaller alternative e-readers, while admitting they weren't for him (he prefers to read on a massive Kindle Scribe). "Are we going to do one? I don't know. Are we looking into them? Yes."

What does "looking into them" mean? Well, "we look into everything," he said, noting Amazon has previously investigated both foldable and rollable e-readers. "But those things are fascinating," he added. "I don't know if [they're] going to be successful, but [they're] definitely worth watching."

title: 10 Apple 'Photos' Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
description: Your Photos library doesn't have to be a mess of screenshots, memes, and bad memories.
fullText:
Apple's Photos app is more than a simple camera roll that eats up all your iCloud storage space. Contrary to popular belief, you can customize the app to make it easier to find the pictures and videos you're looking for, while hidden features help you clean up your storage and keep your media collection organized. If you have an iPhone, these 10 hacks are a must.

The Collections tab in the Photos app arranges itself automatically, showing you suggested photos, memories, and highlight reels at the top. Unfortunately, the way Apple orders things is a bit of a mess. The thing is, Photos has plenty of useful categories and shortcuts for accessing media quickly, such as for screenshots, custom albums, and utilities like Hidden Folder. As such, you should reorder the Collections tab to make it work better for you. Tap the Menu button at the top of the Collections tab and choose Reorder. My advice is to bring the Utilities and Media Types collections to the top, as they serve as useful shortcuts.

If you're like me, your camera roll is filled with too many screenshots, saved photos, memes, GIFs, and videos. They all have their place, but the clutter gets in the way when you want to see or show photos you’ve actually clicked with your iPhone’s camera. As it happens, iOS 27 adds a new feature called "Captured By Me" that only filters photos and videos you’ve shot yourself. If you go to the Collections tab, you’ll find a new Captured By Me section in Utilities. You can also activate this when browsing photos in Library using the Filter button.

Apple’s Photos suggestions are so good, I let the app handle the images that show up on my iPhone and Apple Watch's wallpaper, along with a widget on my iPhone's Home Screen. But suggestions are only as good as your curation. The last thing you want is to see a photo of your ex (or an ex-friend) when you’re trying to get through emails in the morning. If you don’t want to see a person too often, open their photo, tap the Menu button and choose Don’t Feature a Person. You have two choices here. You can either choose Feature This Person Less or Never Feature This Person. The latter option, of course, is best for exes, while the former works better for anyone you don't want to cut out entirely, but would like to see a little bit less of.

The Photos app's Hidden folder is an excellent tool for locking away pictures and videos from your main library. The issue is, the folder might still be accessable by anyone who gets their hands on your iPhone. As such, make sure to lock the Hidden folder behind a Face ID lock to truly protect your sensitive pics. To do so, go to Settings > Apps > Photos > Albums and enable Face ID to automatically enable the hidden folder lock.

Deleted photos aren’t actually deleted—at least, not right away. Apple actually stores deleted photos for 30 days, helpful when you accidentally delete a photo or have second-thoughts, but it’s a double-edged sword. Someone in the know could snoop through your deleted album and retrieve images you assumed were gone forever. These photos and videos are also taking up storage you likely assumed you got back by "deleting" them. As such, make sure to empty the Trash as well. Go to Photos > Utilities > Recently Deleted and tap the Delete All button.

While it’s not the most secure option, keeping some identification documents, passes, or tickets as photos can help in a pinch. It seems like Apple knows that this is a common use case. In iOS 27, if you go to the Collections tab, you’ll find a new Identity Documents section under the Utilities dropdown. When you open it, you’ll find an automatically curated grid of all the photos that contain IDs. If you like this feature, I highly recommend using the first hack in this list to reorder the Collections screen, putting the Identity Documents section right at the top.

iCloud can be a huge help for managing your ever-growing Photos library. As long as you have available cloud storage, photos and videos are uploaded in the background automatically, and if you’re low on storage on your iPhone, "Optimize Storage" automatically offloads the files to the cloud.

Unfortunately, sometimes it doesn’t work when you really want to. Perhaps you want to add photos in a shared album, or you want to see photos on your Mac. But your iPhone is low on battery, or on a spotty connection, so the photos never seem to sync. Now, if you’re running iOS 27, you can use a hidden setting to force iCloud sync. Go to Settings > Photos > Sync Immediately and enable For Today.

When it launched, Apple’s Clean Up tool left something to be desired. It would remove objects, but leave weird shadows or blobs behind. With the release of Apple’s new Siri AI, Clean Up gets a big upgrade—but only if you use Apple’s iCloud servers. (Apple says its service, Private Cloud Compute, secures your data.) As such, Clean Up is now a reliable option to quickly remove objects from your photos. Open an image, tap on Edit, choose the Tools option, and select the Clean Up tool. From the top, make sure to switch to the High-Quality option to use Apple’s servers. Highlight parts to remove, and tap Clean Up. If it’s a heavier edit, you might need to wait for a minute or two. In my experience, the result will be worth it.

It can get tedious to apply the same edits across multiple photos. Luckily, you don't need to waste time fiddling with the same sliders on each image: Photos lets you copy all edits from one image and paste them to multiple photos. To do so, choose your edited photo or video, tap the Menu button, and choose Copy Edits. Then, review and disable any edits you don’t want, and choose Copy. Now, go back to your Library, tap Select, and choose all the photos or videos where you want to apply the same edit. Tap the Menu button and choose Paste Edits to add the same edit settings to all images.

Apple’s Live Text feature turns any text digital. Snap a photo of a menu, and you can copy it. Scan a page, and you can paste it in Notes. But it’s not just limited to the camera or screenshots: It’s integrated directly into the Photos app as well, and arguably, it’s the easiest place to use this feature. When you are viewing an image with text in it, you will see the Live Text icon in the bottom right. Tap on it, and iOS will highlight the text in the image. You can tap and hold to take action on text, and you can easily copy things from here as well.

title: More elite-level events to award equal prize money
description: The Women's Tennis Association confirms all its combined 1000 events will award equal prize money from 2027 in a "major milestone".
fullText:
Men and women will receive equal prize money at all combined 1,000 events - the highest level of competition outside of the Grand Slams - from next year, the Women's Tennis Association (WTA) has announced.

Events at Indian Wells, California, Miami, Madrid and Beijing already met that commitment, as well as all four Grand Slams.

However, the Italian Open, Canadian Open and Cincinnati Open will now also fall into line to meet a long-standing aim of the WTA, at events where men and women both feature.

In 2023, Italian Open organisers had vowed to have equal prize money from 2025 but did not follow through on that pledge.

The total men's prize money this year in Rome was £7.3m while the women received £6.3m.

"Achieving equal prize money across all combined WTA 1,000 tournaments is a major milestone for tennis," said WTA chair Valerie Camillo.

"It demonstrates the WTA's continued commitment to leading the sports industry in delivering our athletes competitive and financial equality and is a testament to the enduring nature of the founding vision of the WTA."

The WTA has also announced adjustments to the calendar to give players greater flexibility.

Those alterations include a reduction - from six to four - in the number of WTA 500-level tournaments players ranked inside the top 50 in the world are mandated to play.

It will also allow players to replace one eligible WTA 1,000 tournament result with a stronger WTA 500 or 250 result on their ranking.

"We have listened to player feedback on the demands of the calendar, and responded with a meaningful reduction in commitments," said Camillo.

American world number three Jessica Pegula said: "The 2027 changes give us more ability to build our seasons around our own goals - competitively and personally.

"That's an impactful step forward for players."

title: Real submit 'substantial' dossier in Barca payments case
description: Real Madrid have sent Uefa "evidence of extraordinary gravity" relating to payments made by Barcelona to a former vice-president of Spain's referees' committee.
fullText:
Real Madrid say they have sent Uefa "evidence of extraordinary gravity" relating to payments made by Barcelona to a former vice-president of Spain's referees' committee.

European football's governing body says it will assess the documents - linked to allegations of 8.4m euros (£7.2m) being paid by Barcelona to Jose Maria Enriquez Negreira between 2001 and 2018 - as part of their ongoing review of the case.

Barcelona have repeatedly denied any wrongdoing since the matter came to light in 2023, stressing that the money paid was for scouting and technical reports provided by Negreira and his Dasnil 95 company about officials.

However, Real say that their new dossier, which is reported to be more than 50,000 pages in length, details contains evidence "which directly affects the integrity of the competition and confidence in the refereeing system".

Uefa described the dossier as "substantial" and said its ethics and disciplinary inspectors will "assess it as part of their ongoing review".

It has been alleged previously that money paid to Negreira was being used to bribe referees, which Barcelona have strenuously denied.

In a statement on Thursday, Real said that they wanted the investigation to progress "as quickly as possible until its complete conclusion" and urged officials to "adopt the corresponding decisions in accordance with the seriousness of the proven facts".

In a statement on Thursday, Barcelona responded by saying that Uefa had "not opened any new proceedings" against them.

They added: "Proceedings were initiated in 2023, with the appointment of two investigators who have since carried out the action they deemed appropriate.

"The club has always complied with all their requests. These proceedings have not been reopened because they have never been closed.

"It is up to the investigators to determine what action, if any, they consider appropriate regarding this documentation. As of today, they have not made any new requests to Barcelona nor have they forwarded Real Madrid's complaint to the club. Should they do so, the club will respond accordingly.

"In accordance with the applicable legislation, this file is subject to the outcome of the criminal proceedings taking place in Spain and will remain therein."

In June 2023, Uefa's investigators decided Barcelona would not face any punishment and they have continued to appear in European competition since then.

A Barcelona court has been looking at the case since the same year and that investigation is still ongoing.

La Liga president Javier Tebas said in March 2023 that the competition body "could not take any action" because it happened too long ago. He said the case was "time-barred in sports law, but not in criminal law".
