title: Space for Gannon-Doak? Does McGinn keep place? Key questions for Pocognoli
description: Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli has decisions to make as he searches for his first win in North Macedonia on Saturday.
fullText:
Nations League: North Macedonia v Scotland

Nacionalna Arena Toše Proeski, Skopje

Two games, one point, no goals. And a home debut hampered by an early red card.

New Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli might have hoped to know more about his side by now. But little was learned at Hampden on Tuesday as his 10-man team were outclassed by Switzerland.

That makes Saturday’s match in North Macedonia - live on the BBC - even more important. A first win under the Belgian is needed.

How might Scotland achieve that? And what are the key questions facing the head coach?

You are the Scotland boss - what would you do?

New coach, new players, but same old failings hamper Scotland

Hampden debut to forget but Pocognoli looks at bigger picture

Goalkeeper Angus Gunn admitted he'd "probably be disappointed" when he looked back at the goals he conceded against the Swiss.

The 30-year-old was Steve Clarke's number one at the World Cup and, since then, has remained in the United States with San Jose Earthquakes.

But a far from successful start at his new club - where he has conceded 23 goals in 11 games - has continued into international duty.

Ricardo Rodriguez's opener was, in pundit Andy Halliday's view, "shoulder height [with] not a lot of pace". Gunn's failure to keep it out was "so poor", he said.

While there was little that could be done for the Swiss' deserved second, the goalkeeper didn't cover himself in glory for the third goal, with Zeki Amdouni's finish going through him.

Gunn's far from convincing performance sparked a conversation around whether he should start on Saturday.

Will Pocognoli change goalkeeper after Swiss loss?

In truth, he probably will due to the lack of better options.

Scott Bain is in the Scottish Premiership with Falkirk, while Jon McCracken is with Bradford in England's League One. Liam Kelly is yet to be anywhere other than the bench for Rangers this term.

But Pocognoli has not shied away from big calls so far - his initial bold squad and his offering of three debuts in two games stand out. It wouldn't be out of the question for him to shake things up in Skopje.

"They were good strikes, but as a goalkeeper, I'm always disappointed when I concede a goal," Gunn acknowledged after facing the Swiss. "I'll look back and see what I could have done better and get better for the next game."

Who knows when that next game will be...

While there is a little uncertainty in goal, Pocognoli may have been given a bit of clarity about the make-up of his defence in his first two games.

Substitute Stephen Welsh was a winner on a grim night against the Swiss.

The Swansea City defender settled nicely into his debut in Slovenia on Saturday on the left side of the back three, and might have felt aggrieved to drop to the bench on Tuesday as the head coach handed a debut to Luis Binks.

But Jack Hendry's red card necessitated a reshuffle and Welsh was restored to the team in a more familiar position on the right and performed admirably again.

Not only is the former Celtic and Motherwell defender vocal and versatile, he is also comfortable carrying the ball - a key asset in Pocognoli's style.

His unexpected home debut ought to help him back into the starting line-up on Saturday, especially with Hendry suspended.

While the second half in Slovenia showed Pocognoli's system can be exciting, it remains unclear if it best suits this Scotland squad?

Two games in and winger Ben Gannon-Doak has yet to start. His impact as a substitute in both has been notable, leading Halliday to say he'd be "shocked" if the Bournemouth player didn't start against Group B1's bottom side.

However, in the Belgian's 3-4-1-2 set-up, there is no obvious place for him. Wing-back would seem the most likely, but the 20-year-old's defensive instincts are not the same as those of Aaron Hickey or Nathan Patterson.

Perhaps Pocognoli needs to be more flexible - something he said he is but has yet to show in his shape. But if he wants to stick to his preference, is this the game to try Gannon-Doak at wing-back?

Gannon-Doak offers an attacking threat like few others do in a Scotland shirt. He could do with a hand from some pals. John McGinn, anyone?

The Aston Villa captain won a bounty of fouls against the Swiss, and though he was much-improved like the rest in the second half at the Stozice Arena, he's still not reaching the levels he does at his Premier League club.

Pocognoli needs more from the Tartan Army talisman as he hurtles towards a century of caps - he's on 91.

The vice-captain is another whose name has been mentioned in the 'does this system suit Scotland' conversation.

It's been a while since McGinn delivered one of those big performances for his country, but his ability to create a moment of magic and drive a team forward makes him difficult to drop.

Another big call for Pocognoli to ponder...

What should be a little more straightforward is giving Kieron Bowie another start.

The Sassuolo striker was sacrificed just over 10 minutes into his first Scotland start to make space for Welsh in defence.

His partnership with Oli McBurnie showed promising signs in the 20 minutes or so they were together in Slovenia, but there was little time to build on that cameo against the Swiss. Surely he and the Hull City striker will get another chance?

If there were any concerns McBurnie wasn't up for the fight - five years on from his last international involvement - they have been quashed in these past two games.

His work-rate as a largely solo striker - hauling his team up and holding the ball in - was commendable. If only Bowie was still on the field for the flurry of flick-ons he won in the first half.

Pocognoli has inherited one of the overriding problems Clarke wrestled with during his spell - scoring goals. That’s four games now without one, and the Scots are just 25 minutes away from setting a new - unwanted - record for failing to score.

In 1970-71, they went 447 minutes without finding the back of the net - it’s been 422 minutes of football since McGinn’s deflected strike against Haiti in Boston.

title: Unheralded Stewart stars at Alfred Dunhill Links
description: On a day when Matt Fitzpatrick began his quest for a fifth win of the year, Robert MacIntyre reacted furiously to a drone and Lee Westwood and Ian Poulter made a DP World Tour return after an absence of almost four years, two players outside the world's top 700 stole the show at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship.
fullText:
Alfred Dunhill Links Championship - round one

-7 M Stewart (Sco), J Buchanan (Aus); -6 MJ Daffue (SA), C Jarvis (SA)

Selected others: -4 M Fitzpatrick (Eng), S Straka (Aut), C Hill (Sco), S Bairstow (Eng); -3 B Koepka (US); -2 T Fleetwood (Eng); -1 A Fitzpatrick (Eng), R MacIntyre (Sco), L Westwood (Eng), I Poulter (Eng); +2 T Hatton (Eng)

On a day when Matt Fitzpatrick began his quest for a fifth win of the year, Robert MacIntyre reacted furiously to a drone and Lee Westwood and Ian Poulter made a DP World Tour return after an absence of almost four years, it was a player from outside the world's top 900 that stole the show at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship.

Scotland's Michael Stewart, ranked 979, shot 65 to sit at seven under after outscoring a big-name field to share the lead at the end of round one.

It gave the Scot a share of the lead after round one, with Australia's Jack Buchanan.

Stewart, 36, has played only five events on the main European circuit - the last in 2023 - and teed off less than 24 hours after finishing second in the Tartan Tour's Duddingston Classic having received a sponsor's invite this week.

However, after making a solitary birdie on the front nine, an eagle on the par-five 12th proved to be the catalyst for him the play the next five holes in six under after the turn.

"It's easy to get yourself up for this event. I played Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday [at Duddingston], straight here. I've played here a lot in the past and just delighted to be part of the event.

"I grew up on a links course. I played nice all day to be honest. Lots of fairways, lots of greens and then on the back, the putter got hot."

Stewart's remarkable back nine at Carnoustie and Buchanan's equally impressive score at Kingsbarns, was in contrast to several eye-catching moments in the team event featuring former sports stars and celebrities, who were paired with the professionals.

However, ex-Real Madrid and Wales winger Gareth Bale did at least provide instantly shareable social media content when his ball found the roof of the Jigger Inn, teeing off on the 17th at St Andrews - one of three courses utilised to stage the tournament.

South Africa's MJ Daffue and Casey Jarvis are a stroke off the lead on the professional leaderboard, while Fitzpatrick, who was victorious at the French Open last week, signed for a four-under 68 to sit three shots adrift.

Five-time major winner Brooks Koepka was three under after a 69 at Carnoustie, a shot better off than Tommy Fleetwood, while defending champion MacIntyre was one under at the same course.

MacIntyre was also spoken to by officials after losing his temper because of a drone flying above him on the par-three eighth, his penultimate hole of the day.

"It drives me insane. I've had previous for it," he said.

"I asked [the rules official] twice previous to the shot on the eighth about the drone. I can't say anything just now.

"He's obviously heard me swear a few times straight at the camera guy. We'll see what the TD [tournament director] has got to say."

Westwood is at one under, with Poulter at level par on their first appearances on the DP World Tour since January 2023, having made controversial switches to LIV Golf in 2022.

title: Second Hull City player crashes near training ground
description: The crash, involving Lucas Gourna-Douath, follows a similar incident involving Sorba Thomas.
fullText:
A Premier League player has been involved in a car crash near Hull City's training ground weeks after a similar incident involving his teammate.

A black Mercedes, which the BBC understands belongs to midfielder Lucas Gourna-Douath, 23, crashed on Millhouse Woods Lane in Cottingham, East Yorkshire.

Pictures of the scene show the car on its side. One person told the BBC that the vehicle had also struck and damaged a resident's car.

Hull City said the club was "aware of images circulating on social media following a road traffic accident near the training ground and can confirm that no one was harmed in the incident".

Humberside Police said emergency services were called at 08:30 GMT.

In September, Gourna-Douath's team-mate Sorba Thomas was involved in a crash on the same road.

Paul Nickerson, who lives on the road from where the incident took place, said: "I arrived just after it turned over because I heard the noise.

"If it had happened a minute before, my wife was walking down the road with our kids taking them to school. So, it's really worrying."

Tracey Evans, who has lived on the road for 19 years, said she has been asking for the speed limit to be reduced for about 10 years.

She said: "At that time, children are coming, going to school, the parents are coming back."

She added measures needed to be put in place "to avoid something happening in the future".

title: Never played in Prem - and now face World Cup hosts
description: Jack Combes and Alex Post tell BBC Sport about a "dream come true" as they look ahead to the 2027 Rugby World Cup opener against hosts Australia.
fullText:
It is 1 October 2027. There are 61,000 fans inside Perth Stadium.

There is a global TV audience in the millions as two teams go through their final warm-ups preparing to open the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

For hosts Australia, twice world champions with a proud rugby history across the codes, it is familiar territory.

For their opponents Hong Kong China, it is anything but.

It will be their World Cup debut and for their players it will be biggest match of their lives.

Among them, all being well, are Jack Combes and Alex Post. Two players more used to the lower semi-professional tiers of the English league system than the global spotlight.

It is David v Goliath - in football parlance it is Spain v Cape Verde. You get the idea.

Twelve months earlier to the day, Jack and Alex are in Hong Kong. It is a national holiday and both have taken time out to tell BBC Sport about how their sporting and personal lives have been transformed.

"I think the whole run-up to the whole qualification process was already a dream in itself. To qualify for a men's first World Cup was huge," said Combes, a scrum-half.

There are glints in their eyes and smiles on their faces - why wouldn't there be?

Hong Kong China have been drawn in Pool A at the World Cup, where not just the hosts await, but also Chile - and the All Blacks.

"People will say it's daunting and it's a huge challenge to have those two top nations in your pool, but if you're going to do it, do it properly. Why not?" said Post.

"People might question whether we deserve to be there. But for me, if you asked anyone as a kid, if you could open up the World Cup in that first game in a year's time, it's genuinely amazing. A dream come true.

"And I'm sure anyone who does give us any criticism about us being there, there's no way they wouldn't be doing the same thing if they could, 100%."

Despite having made his international debut a decade ago, until recently Post was hooking for Richmond in The Champ.

"Unfortunately, I've never played at The Prem level. But The Champ definitely doesn't get the credit it deserves," said the 31-year-old.

"It's a very tough league. And that was great preparation for the international games."

Post was a full-time rugby player with Hong Kong China, before the Covid pandemic brought that to an end and he began a Masters degree at the University of Oxford.

The Varsity match at Twickenham remains one of the larger crowds he has played in front of.

"One of the unique selling points for Hong Kong is the players are contracted all year round and spend all their time together," said Post.

"So it wasn't really feasible for players like myself to stay at Richmond.

"Hong Kong was very much, 'we need boots on the ground'.

"I've moved my family and myself over the last couple of weeks and yeah, kind of chase the dream for the next year."

A full-time professional contract has enabled greater focus on the game away from being a financial analyst.

"With Richmond, we'd train twice a week and then you would do your own gym sessions in your own time," added Post.

"But you can probably do twice as much as that with Hong Kong now."

For Combes, 29, a former student and teacher at Hartpury College, it has been a circuitous route to professional sport that included a spell at Birmingham Moseley in England's third tier.

"So I've been full-time in the sevens for about three and a half years now," he said.

"I've done my career in reverse. I went from teaching after an ACL (anterior cruciate ligament injury), to playing semi-professional rugby, to being a full-time athlete at the age of 25.

"I wouldn't change it for the world, but going into a full-time environment where you have the resources, you have the training time, physical development, it's necessary for what we're facing."

Hong Kong has a proud tradition of rugby stretching back seven decades, not least around its annual sevens tournament.

They qualified for the World Cup by defeating Korea 70-22 in the final round of the Asia Rugby Championship last year.

A late 42-40 victory over fellow World Cup finalists Uruguay in July was perhaps the strongest showing yet of where they stand.

"The mindset's changed from years gone by where you compete in Asia and you play against teams that you know you probably should be beating," said Combes.

"Now we're completely on the other side of the spectrum where we've got nothing to lose.

"I think just be ambitious, be fearless, and go for it.

"'Be memorable' is the phrase that coaches have been talking about."

Both Post and Combes were born in Hong Kong and came up through the age-grade system there. They have witnessed how the game has grown there and are aware of the criticism they have faced, often focused on the international make-up of the team.

"It's always the first criticism we get after an international game," said Post.

"We don't go looking for that criticism or feedback. But it's always going to be there. I think for us, just perform and try and put something out there that people are proud of."

"I was born here in 1997," added Combes.

"Mum is half Chinese and going through the whole minis rugby here where we probably had one of the biggest mini rugby numbers base in the world, up until Covid.

"But I think the game's back growing within local schools - primary, secondary.

"Hopefully we can inspire the next generation."

Former London Irish and Ospreys director of rugby Toby Booth has joined the coaching set-up.

A good test of where they are at will come when Hong Kong China take on three countries in the Nations Cup next month, all with World Cup heritage, in the shape of USA, Canada and Tonga.

"Personally, I've got a whole bunch of pressure just from my family and friends," said Post.

"I've been getting messages all today saying it's one year, you better make the team.

"There will definitely be a big Hong Kong contingent [in Perth]. We want to be everyone's second team."

"You know, we are always going to be the underdogs," said Combes, who is known to his team-mates as Maradona for his keenness to kick any stray footballs that make their way on to the training pitch.

"I think our whole string of games leading into the World Cup with Nations Cup, warm-up games we're always going to be sort of looked over.

"But I think that works in our favour - we're just a bit fearless."

Oh, and remember Spain v Cape Verde at the Fifa World Cup? That ended in a draw.

title: Will 2026 finally be Warrington Wolves' year?
description: Can Super League's perennial nearly side Warrington Wolves get over the line and win a first Grand Final this Saturday?
fullText:
Britain did not have a single motorway in 1955.

We were still five years out from the MOT being introduced and cars did not require a seatbelt.

There was one television channel, provided by the BBC.

Capital punishment was still in place.

The humble postcode had not yet been rolled out across the land.

And rationing was still very much in the national memory, having only been phased out a year beforehand.

All of this paints a picture as to what life was like when Warrington last won a league championship.

On Saturday they stand 80 minutes away from ending a 71-year wait for another title and their boss Sam Burgess has the chance to lay down a marker as a coach just as he did during an illustrious playing career.

But can Super League's perennial nearly side finally get over the line and finally earn a league triumph in the modern era?

Quiz: Name every Super League Grand Finalist

Former England captain Burgess began his career as Warrington head coach in earnest ahead of the 2024 season - off the back of Daryl Powell's uncompetitive stint in charge of the Wire.

A legend of the game as a player, it was his first top job as a coach, five years after he retired following his enviable stint both on the pitch and as assistant coach down under with South Sydney Rabbitohs.

A first Wembley appearance came shortly after, as Wolves reached that season's Challenge Cup final, when they were undone by a Wigan Warriors side on the way to a quadruple.

Twelve months later, treble-winners-in-waiting Hull KR beat them again in the final.

Burgess' side eventually missed out on a play-off spot altogether in 2025, finishing eighth, but, in contrast, they have put together a consistent campaign in 2026 to finish third in the table, behind second-placed Leeds on points difference.

So you might expect Burgess to be feeling rather pleased with himself, and his side, as they prepare for the first Grand Final of his tenure and a meeting with Powell, who has inspired Wakefield's ascent from the Championship to the top of the sport after leaving the Wire.

"Not really," Burgess replied when asked in his pre-match media commitments whether it gave him extra satisfaction that his side had proved him right by emerging as challengers after their disappointing 2025.

"I'm pretty satisfied to be here. I guess I'll find out how satisfied I am on Saturday at about eight o'clock."

Warrington Wolves v Wakefield Trinity

Saturday, 3 October, kick-off 18:00 BST

Listen to commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Radio Merseyside, BBC Radio Leeds and BBC Sounds; watch highlights Saturday, 3 October from 23:00 BST on iPlayer and BBC Two on Sunday at 13:45 BST

It took 14 years into the Super League era before Warrington reached their first Grand Final and this year is the fifth time they have reached Old Trafford, following previous finals in 2012, 2013, 2016 and 2018.

Tony Smith's impressive Wire side came undone against Leeds first and then again at the hands of Wigan in 2013 and 2016 - with Steve Price last leading the club to a Grand Final in 2018 when they were defeated by the Warriors for a third time in a row.

Since that point, the Primrose and Blue have failed to trouble the upper echelons of the sport, with St Helens' dominant spell starting the following year while Wigan and Hull KR have both taken turns at having a commanding stint of their own.

So far this year, they have narrowly missed out on second place in the regular season and dispatched reigning champions Hull KR and Leeds in the play-offs.

Yet when times were tough in 2025, Burgess never gave up and said that it was a belief in his side and the knowledge that Warrington had a long-term plan that kept his camp motivated.

"I could see a lot of green shoots last year where we're going," he added.

"You've got to be able to believe it to do it, and I believed in the club, I believed in the players we had, and I believed in the philosophy that we've got, so I guess we've been very consistent all year without jumping out at anyone, which is a good sign.

"We've had a lot of challenges throughout the year, we've managed them well as a club, which has been important."

Ask those in the know at the beginning of the 2026 season which two teams would contest the Grand Final and not many would have picked out Warrington or Wakefield.

"It's Warrington's year" has become something of a meme in the northern hemisphere's rugby league fandom in the past few years - describing how one of the league's best-funded and well-supported teams always looks the part, but falls at the final hurdle.

Former England coach Steve McNamara arrived at the club as an assistant coach last October following his departure from a spell at Catalans, who he guided to the Challenge Cup and two Super League Grand Finals.

He is set to join Hull FC for next season but Burgess believes their previous failures have not happened in a vacuum - but have shaped the team they have become this season.

"We've played a couple of big games over the last three years, so we've got a bit of experience," said Burgess.

"We have matured as a group and as a club. The club has matured with us, which is important. Whether it counts as much, on Saturday, we'll see."

Of course, Burgess' time as a player can be summed up by a stunning 2014 season which culminated in a victorious NRL Grand Final with the Rabbitohs, when he played on with a broken cheekbone and also won the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.

Asked about how he reflected on that moment ahead of his first Grand Final as a coach, Burgess said: "It's much easier as a player.

"Any experience is experience whether it's as a player, coach, staff member, assistant, whatever. We've got a bit of experience in the room.

"Steve McNamara brought a lot of experience to us this year as well, which is going to help for something.

"We've got a lot of things in our corner. Again, when the whistle blows at six o'clock, you've got to do the right jobs and get the performance on the field."

title: England avoid Australia & India in World Cup draw
description: England avoid defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Cricket World Cup.
fullText:
England have avoided defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup.

India and Pakistan are, once again, placed in the same group, alongside Australia, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and a qualifier.

England, who won the trophy in 2019, are in the same group as co-hosts South Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and a qualifier.

Harry Brook's side, who have enjoyed a resurgence in the 50-over format, begin their campaign against Bangladesh on 8 October, and Sri Lanka on 13 October in Windhoek, Namibia.

They will come up against South Africa in Gqeberha on 16 October before travelling to Harare to face a qualifier on 20 October. They round off the group stage when they face New Zealand, again in Gqeberha, on 23 October.

The visit to Zimbabwe is significant, with England having not played there since 2004.

Political unrest in Zimbabwe under the regime of former president Robert Mugabe caused problems for England's men's team throughout the 2000s.

England boycotted their fixture against Zimbabwe in Harare at the 2003 World Cup - a decision which ultimately derailed their campaign.

Relations have improved in recent years, however, and BBC Sport reported in 2025 that the two cricket boards were discussing a potential England tour of the country in the next cycle of international cricket between 2027 and 2031.

After three matches to decide the final two qualifiers, the tournament group stage will open with a repeat of the 2023 final when India and Australia face each other in Cape Town on 7 October.

Arch-rivals India and Pakistan, who do not play each other outside tournaments, will meet in Johannesburg on 10 October.

The top three, plus the best fourth-placed finisher, from the two groups progress to the Super 7 stage.

From there, the top four teams will qualify for the semi-finals, which are scheduled for 17 and 18 November, before the final on 21 November in Johannesburg.

title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
description: The prime minister said he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners sell up after Premier League rule breaches.
fullText:
Downing Street has said Manchester City are not "above the rules" after Andy Burnham was criticised for his comments about the club's breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The prime minister said on Wednesday he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners decide to sell up after City were found guilty by an independent commission of most of the 115 charges they faced.

His remarks were branded "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary" by the Tories and took many in the football community by surprise.

In a statement following the backlash, Downing Street said the PM had made clear "the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules".

In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City are expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process", saying it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene 

In response, the Tories accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

Man City to argue sponsorship deals came from Abu Dhabi government

Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions

The intricate web Man City spun to con the Premier League

Shadow minister for sport Louie French called for the government to "keep politics out of football and ensure the Premier League's independent commission can do its job free of outside influence".

"The club face unprecedented allegations and fans are horrified by what they are reading in the papers," the Tory MP said.

"Yet Burnham is publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues. Fans will rightly ask whether political pressure is being applied here and how it relates to the owners' well-reported investments in Manchester.

"Football must be governed independently, with the rules applying equally to everyone. Fans deserve confidence that no club or owner is above those rules."

And Lib Dem MP Anna Sabine, the party's spokesperson on sport, said: "Fans of every club deserve to know the rules apply to everyone... Burnham needs to remember he's prime minister for everyone, not just Manchester."

It comes as the chairwoman of the Commons Treasury committee, Labour MP Dame Meg Hillier, wrote to HMRC on Thursday to ask for reassurance that it has "seized of the importance" of the case for any potential tax implications.

In his BBC interview, Burnham also said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners as Greater Manchester mayor would stand up to scrutiny.

He compared City's situation to how the club he supports, Everton, had been charged with a more minor breach of Premier League financial rules in 2023, but said he "hold[s] the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process".

Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.

The independent panel that found City guilty of rule breaches will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment, which could include a huge fine or points deduction.

City have maintained their innocence of all the accusations made.

The chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".

In a statement, David Kogan said the IFR "has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate", while "taking account of the findings made by the Leagues".

He added that proceedings remain ongoing and he hoped for a quick resolution.

title: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of Man City case
description: The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing HMRC, has urged the body to scrutinise tax implications of the Manchester City verdict.
fullText:
Findings from the Premier League's case against Manchester City require scrutiny from His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the chair of a cross-party group of MPs has told the tax authority.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by Friday.

The club were found to have artificially inflated revenue through "sham" sponsorship agreements with the help of their owners.

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of HMRC, has therefore asked whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

The letter follows a report from the Tax Policy Associates, external which claims City failed to pay as much as £12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini.

In addition to unpaid income tax and National Insurance, the report claims City could face a penalty charge that would take their liabilities to £24m.

Manchester City vs The Premier League

Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks

Manchester City will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.

This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.

However, as first reported by the Daily Mail and Times, sources have told BBC Sport that City are expected to tell an appeal board that they have evidence showing the money directed to state-owned sponsors came from the Abu Dhabi government, rather than from ADUG.

Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.

In its 40-page decision, the independent commission detailed how City had "denied there had ever been any disguised funding scheme of the type alleged by the Premier League. Its case was that [it] had misunderstood how Abu Dhabi sponsorship agreements had been funded... The reality was [the club contested] that Abu Dhabi sponsors had always been liable for all recorded sponsorship fees and all had in fact been paid to the club by Abu Dhabi sponsors from their own funds/resources.

"No part of any recorded sponsorship fee had been paid by ADUG or from using ADUG funds. Abu Dhabi sponsors had from time to time applied for financial assistance from the Abu Dhabi government toward their liability to pay the recorded sponsorship fees - such applications had been granted…"

The independent commission rejected this submission as "untrue", saying: "We concluded that it was an 'explanation' that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme."

City's argument is likely to lead to renewed debate over the extent to which City's ownership is separate from the Abu Dhabi state, and over the ramifications of club ownership with state connections.

Mansour is a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi, and the brother of UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Since the takeover in 2008, City have insisted the club is a completely private enterprise, and not state-owned. However, some critics have questioned the distinction, with human rights campaigners claiming the ownership of City has been used to "sportswash" the UAE.

On Saturday, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak referred to "irrefutable evidence" that he claimed supports the club's claims of innocence. City have claimed the commission's decision contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

It has emerged that Al Mubarak, who was appointed chairman of City following the takeover in 2008, is named as an Emirati diplomat on the UK government's current directory of all foreign representatives.

Representatives of foreign states and their diplomatic staff "enjoy privileges and immunities under the Diplomatic Privileges Act (1964)", giving diplomats immunity from prosecution under criminal, civil and administrative laws.

City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".

The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.

The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport.

Additional reporting from James Landale, diplomatic correspondent for BBC News.

title: Ryan Spooner Hangs Up Skates After 41-Goal Bruins Run
description: Ryan Spooner retires from hockey. The former Bruin scored 41 goals in Boston. See the stats and why his quiet leadership mattered most.
fullText:
The party is over for Ryan Spooner. The former Boston Bruins forward officially announced his retirement on Tuesday after playing his final season in Slovakia. He walked away from the game after a long journey that started with a second-round pick in 2010. Spooner never became the superstar some expected, but he left a mark that goes beyond just the numbers. He scored 41 goals for Boston and played 253 games in the black and gold.

Spooner's career was a roller coaster of trades. He went from the Bruins to the Rangers, then to the Oilers, and finally the Canucks before heading overseas. He played in the KHL and Swiss leagues for years after leaving the NHL. His best season away from Boston came in 2023-24 with Omsk Avangard, where he netted 23 goals. But the real story isn't about the stats he piled up in Russia. It is about how he acted when he was a backup in Boston.

Marco Sturm, the current head coach, worked closely with Spooner's teammate Joonas Korpisalo and shared high praise for the quiet players in the locker room. According to a report by Jack Studley on X, Sturm said of Korpisalo's style, which mirrored Spooner's: "What I didn't know at first, because he was that quiet, how popular he was in the room. I give him a lot of credit by not just being a good backup, but also being a good teammate."

That kind of leadership is rare. You do not see it every day in a tough hockey town. Spooner was the guy who showed up every single day and did his job without needing the spotlight. He made the guys around him better just by being there. That is worth more than a single goal.

Let's look at the hard facts from his time in Boston. Spooner had 101 assists to go with his 41 goals for a total of 142 points. He also logged 143 hits and blocked 61 shots. These are not the numbers of a lazy player. They belong to someone who fought for every inch of ice. He even played in the 2017 playoffs, recording two assists in four games.

The end of his career came quickly after a short stint with HK Dukla Trencin. He played five games this season before hanging up the skates. In a press release translated by Google, Spooner thanked the fans and said ending his career was not an easy decision. He believed he could play one more season but felt it was the right time to stop. That honesty is refreshing in a sport full of excuses.

The Bruins need more guys like him now. The team just saw Fraser Minten score his first goal of the 2026-27 season to beat the Rangers, a game where the team won 11 straight at home to start the year. Minten signed a seven-year, $50 million deal this summer. But money does not buy the grit Spooner showed. The new roster has talent, but it needs that quiet, hard-working spirit to win in the playoffs.

Spooner's legacy is simple. He was a good teammate who gave everything he had. The Bruins won't forget the 41 goals, but they will miss the guy who made the room better.

title: Red Sox star Willson Contreras speaks up on ‘data’ and ‘computers after series loss to Yankees
description: As the Boston Red Sox’s 2026 season ended with a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series, veteran catcher Willson Contreras made his frustration with the organization’s data-driven approach clear after Wednesday’s loss. Contreras had momentarily given Boston a glimmer of hope in the sixth inning when he […] The post Red Sox star Willson Contreras speaks up on ‘data’ and ‘computers after series loss to Yankees appeared first on ClutchPoints.
fullText:
Red Sox star Willson Contreras speaks up on 'data' and 'computers after series loss to Yankees appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

As the Boston Red Sox's 2026 season ended with a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series, veteran catcher Willson Contreras made his frustration with the organization's data-driven approach clear after Wednesday's loss.

Contreras had momentarily given Boston a glimmer of hope in the sixth inning when he launched a Statcast-projected 387-foot solo home run to right-center with two outs. The blast ended a 26-inning postseason scoring drought for the Red Sox dating back to Game 2 of last year's Wild Card Series, also against the Yankees. However, New York answered with six runs in the bottom of the inning, turning the game into a 9-2 defeat.

Boston was outscored 18-2 across the two games and was eliminated before getting a chance to play in October. The loss also extended the Red Sox's streak to five consecutive seasons without postseason baseball at Fenway Park.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

After the game, Contreras was asked about manager Chad Tracy's decision to remove starter Sonny Gray in the fifth inning. Gray had allowed six hits across 4 2/3 innings and surrendered only one run, a solo homer by Luis García Jr. He left after reaching 70 pitches with runners on the corners and two outs.

Tracy replaced Gray with left-handed reliever Erik Miller to face Cody Bellinger. Miller surrendered a run-scoring single to Bellinger before allowing another single to García. Gray had recorded a .180/.235/.280 slash line against hitters during their third time facing him this season, while Bellinger had been better against left-handed pitching than right-handed pitching. Contreras responded to the question about Gray by pretending to zip his mouth closed.

He was more direct when discussing Boston's broader reliance on data and technology.

"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball," said Contreras. "The data is here to help us but at the end of the day, you're going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but I'll state it like that."

Willson Contreras: "It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball. The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff I… pic.twitter.com/MS7u5yy96y

— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 1, 2026

The comments came after the Red Sox's disappointing postseason exit and a regular season that featured major swings in performance. Boston fell into a 32-46 hole before going 32-5 from June 25 through August 7, including a franchise-tying 15-game winning streak.

The team then slumped during the final month amid injuries and offensive problems, which carried into the postseason. The Red Sox's bullpen also labored through a second consecutive difficult night against New York, while Garrett Crochet's return from shoulder and lat issues lasted less than an inning. Making his first appearance since April 25, Crochet failed to record an out and was charged with four runs.

Contreras' comments only added to the fallout from an elimination that exposed disagreements over Boston's decision-making and approach under chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.

title: Troubled Gateshead fail to pay September wages
description: Gateshead's players and staff do not receive their September wages on time in the same week major funding is withdrawn from the club.
fullText:
Troubled National League side Gateshead have failed to pay players and staff their wages for September.

The club are bottom of the league and have lost their past five games, conceding 16 goals and scoring just once.

Earlier this week, Mark Nellist resigned from the board of directors and withdrew his funding support, citing that the Tyneside club was "not heading in the direction I would have liked or hoped for".

But the Heed's interim chairman Graham Wood said he was hopeful of quickly finding new investment for the club.

"Following Mark Nellist's sudden decision to withdraw his funding support for the club we have been fully focused on seeking new investment," he said.

"Significant progress has been made in the past 24 hours and we are hopeful of making an announcement in the next day or so.

"Meanwhile, to facilitate our efforts, Mark has agreed to make his shares available for a nominal sum."

Lee Cattermole's side next face Worthing at home on Saturday.

title: Why penalty for Williamson handball was correct call
description: Arsenal defender Leah Williamson was at the heart of a bizarre incident in their Women's Champions League draw with Paris FC.
fullText:
A bizarre error from Arsenal defender Leah Williamson proved costly in their 2-2 draw with Paris FC on Wednesday in the Women's Champions League.

With the Gunners leading 2-1 late on, England captain Williamson stopped a short goal-kick with her hand - believing it had not been taken and that she was to take it - resulting in a penalty being awarded to the hosts, converted by Maeline Mendy.

The unusual incident means the Gunners are fourth in the Champions League table after their opening two games, but would have been second with a victory in the French capital.

After the ball had gone out of play for a goal-kick, Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez played a quick, short pass to Williamson.

Williamson had her arm stretched out to stop the ball and place it so that she could take the goal-kick herself.

With the ball being still and on the field of play when Rodriguez played the ball to Williamson, that was deemed to be the goal-kick instead of Williamson's attempt.

Therefore Williamson was penalised for handball and Mendy levelled the match from the penalty spot.

While Arsenal felt aggrieved at the decision, the guidance on such incidents state that the decision to award a penalty was correct.

Guidance from Law 16 of the International Football Association Board's (Ifab) laws of the game state: "In goal-kick restarts, if the ball is stationary within the goal area and is kicked by any defending player, the goal-kick is considered to have been taken.

"If, after the ball is in play, [a player] commits a handball offence, a penalty kick is awarded if the offence occurred inside the kicker's penalty area.

Law 12 from Ifab also states: "It is an offence if a player deliberately touches the ball with their hand/arm."

In November 2024, Aston Villa defender Tyrone Mings committed an identical error in a Champions League match against Club Brugge.

Brugge won a penalty that was scored by Hans Vanaken, with the Belgian side winning the match 1-0.

"The biggest mistake I witnessed in my career," said Villa boss Unai Emery at the time.

Earlier that year, Gunners centre-back Gabriel also made the mistake in a Champions League match against Bayern Munich.

However in that instance, Arsenal were given the chance to retake the goal-kick.

"He [Gabriel] touched the ball with the hand because he thought it was not in game, but it was in game and the referee admitted it was in game and was handball," said then Bayern boss Thomas Tuchel.

The now England head coach also said that the error in not awarding Bayern a penalty was a "kid's mistake".

Arsenal's assistant coach Aaron D'Antino conducted post-match media duties and explained that, while the intention was for Williamson to take the goal-kick, they will use the incident as a learning experience.

"If we're looking at what we can control, it's just passing the ball to Leah from what I remember seeing. The ball was still rolling and she [Rodriguez] was moving it to Leah for her to take the goal-kicks as we normally do," said D'Antino.

"So maybe the learning in that is how we get the ball to Leah, so we don't put ourselves in that situation."

Former Arsenal and Scotland defender Jen Beattie felt the referee Iuliana Demetrescu got the decision wrong, despite the correct applications of the laws.

"For me, I just don't even know how that happens. Leah knows it's a goal-kick, she's catching the ball. That's shocking from the referee," Beattie told Paramount+.

"I would have been fuming and I would have been embarrassed if they gave that. This is not what they're trying to do. It's just beyond frustrating that that's how they've tied the game.

"Leah's obviously going [to do that] because she's going to take the goal-kick, not because she's worried about the press or trying to change it - or panicking in any situation. Leah Williamson doesn't panic in those moments, she knows what she's doing. The goalkeeper knows what she's doing as well.

"The referee has miscalled it."

title: 2027 NFL Draft stock watch features 11 players on the rise
description: Who are the biggest risers in the 2027 NFL Draft so far? Two quarterbacks have helped their stock significantly with their early showings.
fullText:
As some of the marquee 2027 NFL Draft prospects have faltered in the first month of the season, other players have capitalized on the opportunity to raise their profile.

The group of prospects expected to join the pros next April features a good amount of established stars, from quarterbacks Arch Manning and Dante Moore to wide receiver Jeremiah Smith, among others. But while Smith has continued to set college football ablaze in what is almost assuredly his final campaign, the early results have been decidedly more mixed for several of his peers.

Nevertheless, September often marks the start of a steady ascent in the draft for several players. This year is no different, with a group of standouts already on the upswing.

Here's a closer look at 11 players whose early play has earned them the label of draft risers in the opening stretch of the fall:

An undersized passer who will be 25 before his rookie season and started off in Division II would typically seem like an odd figure to factor heavily into one of the most highly anticipated quarterback classes in years. Indeed, Chambliss still amounted to something of a side attraction entering this year. In continuing his full-on star turn, though, the 6-0, 208-pound passer could force teams to have some uncomfortable reconsiderations of when the circumstances are right to break from protocol and pursue an outlier. Despite playing a brutal early slate, Chambliss has racked up 12 touchdowns and carried Mississippi, proving he can excel even without Lane Kiffin's touch. Not all of his playmaking skills will translate to the NFL, but in a league where offenses place a premium on big gains, coaching staffs should covet Chambliss' calculated aggressiveness both from within and out of structure. His resiliency and decisiveness are also major strong suits. Now firmly out of range for being considered merely a developmental option or an entertaining backup, Chambliss is sure to test the creativity and adaptability of front offices as the pre-draft process continues.

Stats can hardly tell a complete story for any college quarterback, especially in a small sample size that hasn't entailed facing top competition. Still, it's impossible not to take notice of Mensah's masterful start in Miami, during which he's thrown more touchdowns (14) than incompletions (12). Exhibiting command and poise is essential for the Tulane and Duke transfer, who only has pedestrian physical tools when compared to some of the other more gifted throwers in this class. Mensah will also have to show more comfort working down the field and to the sidelines after primarily attacking short - and an understandable way to weaponize Malachi Toney - and over the middle. But if he continues to make great strides with his processing and decision-making against much firmer competition, he'll spark some compelling conversations about his placement in the quarterback pecking order.

With Baugh, Mississippi's Kewan Lacy and Missouri's Ahmad Hardy all putting forth compelling cases entering the season, the battle to be the first running back selected in 2027 figured to make for a fierce competition. Baugh, however, has seemingly cut that debate short. Through four games, he's been borderline unstoppable, rushing for a Football Bowl Subdivision-high 600 yards and 11 touchdowns. The 6-1, 225-pound ball carrier already had all the trappings of a workhorse back. This fall, though, he's ripped off a run of 50 yards or 

Chambliss might be the catalyst for Mississippi's attack, but electric pass catchers are required to make the most of the quarterback's daring tendencies. Having risen from an integral part of a robust receiver room to the focal point of the passing attack, Alexander is more than doing his part to make good on Chambliss' deep-ball prowess. The former Wake Forest transfer has racked up 429 yards - the second most in the Southeastern Conference - and four touchdowns in four games. His background as a high school track standout in Georgia is readily evident on every snap, as he's particularly adept at getting corners to bite at the faintest sign of a fake or hesitation before racing past them downfield. The 6-0, 180-pound target might need to fill out his frame a bit more and demonstrate he can consistently conquer press coverage, but his game-breaking potential should have him rocketing up draft boards.

With Jordyn Tyson off to the Saints, the Sun Devils reloaded at receiver by inking two major transfers in Harris and Omarion Miller. The latter figured to be the more consequential move for next year's draft, but the former is making a far bigger splash early in the season. Harris has accounted for 374 receiving yards - nearly half of his team's total output - along with five touchdown catches. His deep-threat credentials had already been established at Boston College, but the 6-5, 220-pound pass catcher is reinforcing his field-stretching skills by averaging 17.4 yards per reception. In a receiver class that lacks much clarity beyond the top trio of Smith, Coleman and Becker, Harris has mounted a push for a spot in the top 50 - and possibly consideration even earlier.

Does college football have a sufficient supply of talented tight ends to satisfy the NFL's uptick in demand at the position? Beyond Oregon's Jamari Johnson and LSU's Trey'Dez Green, this year's group doesn't seem to measure up to the one teams flocked to in April. The emergence of Reynolds, however, has helped quell some concerns about depth in the upcoming draft. As one of a horde of former Penn State players who followed James Franklin to Virginia Tech, the former five-star recruit has found his footing in a new setting, needing just four games to set career highs with 30 catches, 280 yards and four touchdowns. The 6-4, 250-pound target can't measure up to Johnson or Green as an athletic marvel, but he's nimble enough to free himself from coverage and pick up additional yards after the catch. And with his comfort working as an inline blocker, Reynolds should be an attractive option for a team looking to round out and diversify its offense.

With bookend offensive tackles Francis Mauigoa and Markel Bell both departing as early NFL draft picks, Miami could have been forgiven if it struggled with pass protection in the early going this season. Okunlola ensured that didn't happen. The 6-6, 330-pound blocker stepped in at left tackle and has been superlative from the start, helping keep Mensah as part of a front that has allowed just three total sacks on 136 total dropbacks thus far. Some more refinement would serve the first-year starter well, but a former five-star recruit who was nicknamed "The Pancake Honcho" shouldn't require a hard sell for teams if he keeps playing like this.

Put Johnson anywhere along the front and he's bound to excel. The third-year starter has played at every spot except right guard during his time at Minnesota and made another switch last week, moving back to center from left guard. The result: The 6-6, 325-pound blocker was named the Outland Trophy National Player of the Week. Though his best work has come as a forceful presence in the ground game, Johnson has also helped put statuesque pocket passer Drake Lindsey at ease. Considered by some as a fringe first-round prospect entering the year - he checked in at No. 28 to the Bills in my preseason mock draft - Johnson now might be firmly in Day 1 territory.

It should come as little surprise that a former basketball standout who played just one year of high school football might need some time before fully coming into his own against top college competition. Thompkins showed promise in stretches in 2024-25 after playing in just three games during his first two years at USC, but he's taken his game to a distinct new level after transferring to Alabama. Through four games, he's already matched his previous career high with three sacks on the season. Thompkins is far more nimble and explosive than one might expect of a 6-5, 300-pound defensive linemen. He might not be a fit for every team given his body type and skill set, but he could be a considerably disruptive force as a 3-4 defensive end or defensive tackle in a defense that allows him to get upfield.

With offenses across the NFL shifting back to more under-center looks, it might not be long before teams scramble to add hyperathletic linebackers as a necessary countermeasure for the schematic swing. Cole might be exactly what those defenses are in search of. The 6-3, 235-pounder already demonstrated his ample pursuit speed and bend last season, when he led the Bulldogs with 4 1/2 sacks as a backup. Now, however, he's getting to showcase the full extent of his abilities, as his size and fluidity allow him to stick with running backs and tight ends in coverage or chase down ball carriers to either sideline. He also served up a reminder of just how uniquely explosive he is for his position when he scooped up Oklahoma quarterback John Mateer's fumble and raced 85 yards to the end zone with it, pulling away from his opponents like a wide receiver breaking free from an overmatched corner.

CHRIS COLE HOUSE CALL 🏠

📺: ESPN pic.twitter.com/wNOacZCjqI

In snagging five interceptions in his first three games, Lopa, the 6-5, 210-pound safety, has stepped to the forefront as one of college football's most scintillating young defensive playmakers. The Oregon transfer is still in need of some seasoning after playing sparingly in his first two years with the Ducks. His tackling, in particular, isn't yet up to par, as he can struggle when forced to come to balance and finish off plays even when he's in position to do so. But defensive backs with his size, movement ability and ball skills are rare, and teams are sure to be drawn to what he can offer as a versatile piece in coverage.

title: Real Madrid superstar’s post-injury vacation approved by Mourinho and the club – report
description: Real Madrid ace Kylian Mbappe escaped with a minor injury in France’s first game of the international break and was relieved from national team duty immediately by the manager Zinedine Zidane.The cu...
fullText:
Real Madrid ace Kylian Mbappe escaped with a minor injury in France's first game of the international break and was relieved from national team duty immediately by the manager Zinedine Zidane.

The current diagnosis is of a posterior capsule hyperextension of the left knee, and his recovery time is estimated to be in weeks.

Yet, it could well have been much worse and it is said that the player may well have required surgery if he had played longer.

Currently, the player continues to be in France and has not returned to Madrid.

He has been spotted with his friends and his partner, and it has unsurprisingly led to a lot of speculation on why he is on vacation when he should be working on his return.

Mourinho has backed Mbappe's time off. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

As confirmed by AS in a recent update, however, Mbappe's trip to his country and the time he is enjoying off with his partner and friends is not secretive. In fact, the club completely backed his vacation.

Jose Mourinho is aware of the player taking some time off in France, as are the coaching staff and the medical team of the club.

They all understand that Mbappe's setback only requires rest and that the player returning to the Valdebebas may serve no real purpose.

His recovery plan, in that sense, is said to be 'co-ordinated' and 'consensual' as they describe it in the club offices.

The idea is that he will take his recovery slow and pace it out, likely even missing the team's first game after the break.

Having Mbappe fit for the Clasico is the priority. (Photo by Yasser Bakhsh/Getty Images)

Real Madrid's first game after the break is against Villarreal, and Mourinho and Co. prioritise the player being available in the long run over him being fit for the game against the Yellow Submarines.

The goal, quite clearly, is to have Mbappe fit and raring for the game against Barcelona later in October and the management considers his presence on that night to be fundamental.

So far, the Frenchman has been Real Madrid's top finishing presence in the opposition box and has carried Real Madrid's attack alongside Jude Bellingham.

The sensible idea, in that sense, would be to keep him fit and ready for the big games against Roma, Barcelona and RB Leipzig.

title: Travis Kelce Makes Strong Chiefs Demand Amid NFL Season
description: Kenneth Walker III continues to impress with his strong start this season with the Kansas City Chiefs. fullText:
Kenneth Walker III continues to impress with his strong start this season with the Kansas City Chiefs. He has left many in awe of his elite skill set, including his teammate, Travis Kelce. The veteran tight end shared his demand for the reigning Super Bowl MVP on his Instagram story.

Kansas City owns a 3-0 record and is coming off a 24-10 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. Walker shined anew with 18 rushing attempts for 70 yards and one touchdown. Patrick Mahomes led the offense by completing 20-of-24 passes for 246 yards and two touchdowns against one interception. Kelce finished with two receptions for yards and one score.

Walker's addition has given Mahomes another proven weapon he can maximize. The former Seattle Seahawks star is leading the NFL in rushing yards through three weeks, amassing 360. He is also among the favorites to win some individual honors.

Kelce's story showed him on the field with Walker. He added a caption that showed the level of trust he has and how impressed he is with his new teammate.

Give 9⃣ the ball!!!" Kelce wrote.

Listen to what Travis Kelce is saying: Keep feeding Kenneth Walker the ball! #ChiefsKingdom
(Via killatrav on Instagram) pic.twitter.com/6BpWMXK86g

— Eddie (@EddieRes) September 30, 2026

Kelce and the Chiefs missed the playoff last season, with Mahomes suffering an ACL and LCL injury in December. The star quarterback is now fully recovered and aiming to prove that they are still Super Bowl contenders. title: Bills react to tough start for Patriots QB Drake Maye
description: Buffalo Bills DC Jim Leonhard, New England Patriots QB Drake Maye on division matchup
fullText:
The Bills open division play Sunday against a quarterback off to the worst stretch of his career, and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard is treating him like a problem anyway.

Buffalo's coaching staff met with reporters Monday to close the book on the Week 3 win over the Los Angeles Chargers and turn the page to the first divisional game of the season against the New England Patriots. The biggest topic was New England quarterback Drake Maye, who makes for a "tricky" evaluation this week, per Leonhard.

Maye was in the MVP conversation last season, ranking third in passing touchdowns (31), leading the NFL in passer rating (113.5), completion percentage (72%) and finished tied for lead in win percentage (.824). This against what many considered to be an easy schedule, before getting cooked by the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl.

He has since thrown one touchdown pass against six interceptions and been sacked nine times through three games. That is a far cry from the player Leonhard spent late January getting ready to face in the AFC Championship.

"You turn on the tape from last year, and it was dynamic," the Bills DC said. "We played him in Denver, obviously at the end of the year, and you got to see the best version of what he was going into that game."

Last season, Maye threw for nearly 4,400 yards with 31 passing touchdowns and four rushing scores while carrying the Patriots to an AFC East title and a Super Bowl appearance. The playoffs went the other way: Denver held him without a touchdown and dropped him five times in the AFC Championship, and Seattle picked him off twice while sacking him six more times in the Super Bowl.

He sees the matchup against Buffalo as an opportunity to right the ship.

"This is an opportunity to band together and realize that the best football that we play is together and realizing that starts with me with protecting the football and protecting this team," Maye said. "That's my job, and I've been failing to do that."

Leonhard called Maye's postseason slide — four interceptions and 21 sacks across four games — "slip ups" next to "MVP level" regular-season film, and the struggles have bled into 2026. Maye and the Patriots arrive in Buffalo with the league's lowest-scoring offense at 12.0 points per game.

"You're watching a guy now that's you can tell he's going through some stuff and struggling a little bit, but at the same time he drops back and hits his top step and lets one rip and it's an explosive play," he added.

"You just have to put some pressure on him and hope that the trend continues. Great players are eventually going to come out the other side. You just hope it's after you play them."

The Bills head coach shared his thoughts on facing the Patriots QB with the press today as well.

"It is a week to week-to-week league, and it is so hard to play the position," Joe Brady said. "Drake Maye, he's an outstanding quarterback, he's played for so long at such a high level, he is going to present so many issues for us this week."

title: Justin Jefferson Injury Update: Vikings WR’s Week 4 Status Revealed
description: Justin Jefferson is arguably the best wide receiver in the NFL, but the former first-round pick suffered an ankle injury against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and could not return to the game. The fifth wide receiver taken in the 2025 NFL Draft, Justin Jefferson quickly established himself as one of the biggest steals in his …
fullText:
Justin Jefferson is arguably the best wide receiver in the NFL, but the former first-round pick suffered an ankle injury against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and could not return to the game. The fifth wide receiver taken in the 2025 NFL Draft, Justin Jefferson quickly established himself as one of the biggest steals in his draft class. Appearing in all 16 games while making 14 starts, the rookie finished his inaugural campaign with 88 receptions for 1,400 yards and seven touchdowns.

He continued to dominate from there, earning First-Team All-Pro honors on two separate occasions while leading the league in receptions (128) and yards (1,809) in 2022. The 2025 season was a relative down year as he struggled to develop a rapport with quarterback J.J. McCarthy, but he still ended the season with 84 receptions for 1,048 yards and two touchdowns. While Justin Jefferson looked like his old self in the first two weeks of the season, he suffered an ankle injury early in Week 3 and could not return to the field. While this won't be a long-term injury, the superstar wideout did not practice yesterday and could miss Week 4's contest against the Miami Dolphins.

It's hard to overstate just how unfortunate a serious Justin Jefferson injury would be for the Minnesota Vikings, and how lucky the team is that this isn't a long-term issue. Even with the star wide receiver in the lineup, Minnesota's passing attack hasn't looked all too dominant thus far in the season. Starting quarterback Kyler Murray suffered a concussion early in Week 1, forcing journeyman Carson Wentz to finish the contest and start Week 2. While Murray returned to the lineup in Week 3, he didn't look all too impressive. Playing most of the contest without Justin Jefferson, the quarterback completed just 15 of his 29 attempts for 168 yards, one touchdown, and one interception.

The Minnesota Vikings are a worse team without Justin Jefferson in the lineup, but they probably won't need him to win in Week 4. The Miami Dolphins are perhaps the worst team in football, and Jefferson probably won't be the difference between a win and a loss. There is no such thing as an easy win in the NFL, but Minnesota is considerably more talented and should comfortably win this contest.

The talented wide receiver could provide another dynamic option for an offense looking to strengthen its passing game and compete at the highest level.

Thomas has already demonstrated the ability to become a significant weapon since entering the NFL. His combination of size, speed and big-play ability makes him an intriguing target for teams searching for a proven receiver capable of creating separation and stretching defenses.

Pittsburgh could make sense because of the team's need for additional firepower at wide receiver. The Steelers have continued to build an offense capable of competing in a physical AFC, and adding a player with Thomas' skill set could give the passing attack another dimension.

A move for Thomas would also give Pittsburgh a receiver capable of complementing its existing offensive personnel. His ability to threaten defenses vertically could create more opportunities underneath while forcing opposing defensive backs to account for another dangerous target on every passing play.

Pittsburgh was named one of the best trade spots for Thomas. This is detailed 

With every wideout outside of Wilson failing to meet even modest expectations, Pittsburgh's brass must make a bold move on the trade market. Thomas may not be succeeding with the Jacksonville Jaguars, but his best football should still be ahead of him.

Getting to play with a 10-time Pro Bowl quarterback within an offense that is desperate for pass-catching assistance may be exactly what BTJ needs to turn things around.

At worst, the Steelers cough up a bit of capital for yet another underwhelming wideout who fails to pan out for them. At best, Thomas becomes the new No. 1 WR in Pittsburgh's offense and retains that role for multiple seasons.

A Thomas trade is worth the risk and could pay massive dividends for a Steelers squad looking to take the next step after years of mediocrity.

fullText:
The San Francisco 49ers have quickly established themselves as one of the NFL's biggest stories through the opening three weeks of the 2026 season. With an undefeated record and an offense producing at a high level despite significant injuries, San Francisco has made a major jump in the latest power rankings.

The 49ers improved to 3-0 after defeating the Arizona Cardinals 36-30 in a divisional battle that tested their ability to finish games. Brock Purdy continued to lead an efficient offense, while San Francisco's ability to overcome injuries at wide receiver has made its unbeaten start even more notable.

National evaluations have reflected the team's strong opening month, with several power rankings placing San Francisco near the top of the league. The 49ers have moved ahead of several established contenders because of their combination of offensive production, consistency and an ability to win despite obstacles.

Purdy has been central to that success, particularly with the team's receiving corps dealing with injuries. His strong decision-making and efficiency have allowed the offense to remain productive, while the offensive line has provided the quarterback with enough time to operate effectively.

Purdy and company have taken the second spot in the latest power rankings. This can be seen in an analysis by Nick Wagoner for ESPN.

Week 3 result: Beat the Cardinals 36-30
Week 3 ranking: 3

Fantasy surprise: TE George Kittle

Under normal circumstances, it would not be a surprise to see Kittle as the TE4 in fantasy. But given that he tore his right Achilles on Jan. 11 and missed all of training camp, that he returned in Week 1 close to his usual self is a testament to his passion for the game. And the Niners have needed every bit of his production to help weather the storm of injuries elsewhere. Kittle ranks fifth among all tight ends in receiving yards (174), 11th in receptions (12) and tied for first in touchdowns (three).

There are still questions that San Francisco will need to answer as the schedule becomes more demanding. Injuries remain a concern, and the defense has not always produced the same level of dominance expected from a championship-caliber team, meaning the 49ers will face tougher tests as the season progresses.

For now, however, the undefeated start has placed San Francisco firmly in the NFL's contender conversation. With the 49ers preparing to face the Denver Broncos in Week 4, another strong performance could further strengthen their position near the top of the league's power rankings.
